# The Power Watershed as a Differentiable Segmentation Layer

**Abstract.** Can a Watershed transform, the classical tool of morphological segmentation, be placed at the end of a deep network and trained through? The Power Watershed (PW) is the \(p\rightarrow\infty\) limit of the seeded Random Walker (RW) with edge weights raised to the power _p_. At every finite _p_ the RW solves a sparse positive-definite linear system and is exactly differentiable with respect to the edge weights and the unaries through one adjoint solve; its multi-label form costs one right-hand side per label, and its limit is the PW. We study this family as the last layer of a segmentation network, the watershed layer (WS layer). A conditioning study measures how the solve, the gradient and the distance to the limit evolve with _p_, and the implicit gradient is checked against unrolling. On synthetic data with correct edge costs the WS layer transforms a soft prediction into an exact boundary. On nuclei segmentation (PanNuke), a binary WS layer is level with a thresholded U-Net. With the instances as labels, the WS layer turns the U-Net into an instance segmenter whose number of labels is set per image by the markers rather than by the output layout, and the network is trained through that partition: instance _F_<sub>1</sub> rises from 0.656 to 0.795 over a U-Net with connected components, level with the same network followed by a tuned marker watershed. At the training temperature the partition is a watershed of the learned costs, and the finite temperature lets the solve hedge, discounting weak markers and sharing contested pixels. The hedging puts the WS layer 0.015-0.020 _F_<sub>1</sub> ahead of the baseline when trained on a tenth of the data, at the price of having to deploy the finite-p solve rather than its exact limit at inference.  and the full experimental record are released. **Keywords:** Morphological segmentation \(\cdot\) Random Walker \(\cdot\) differentiable segmentation \(\cdot\) instance segmentation \(\cdot\) deep unrolling.

### 1 Introduction

Deep segmentation networks such as U-Nets perform well under supervision but have many parameters, which reduces explainability, and produce soft, per-pixel

<tbc>outputs. Boundaries come out rounded, output potentials are rarely binary, and the number of labels is fixed by a one-hot channel layout decided at design time. Watersheds have the opposite profile: results are crisp and directly explainable through labelling and the topographical nature of the input data. As a result, boundaries appear on the strongest edges of a cost map, regions are piecewise constant, and the number of regions is equal to the number of markers, not a property of the algorithm. An interesting combination is thus to add a watershed at the end of a segmenting network and train through it. The obstacle is that a watershed is a combinatorial procedure on a graph, with a gradient that is zero almost everywhere.

This article makes the case that the Power Watershed framework of Couprie et al. [13,14] can be used in this context. It provides its own relaxation, the Random Walker [21] at finite _p_, and we evaluate what the resulting watershed layer (WS layer) can be used for. The framework minimises \(\sum_ew_e^p|x_u-x_v|^q\) over potentials _x_ fixed on seeds; _q_=2 with finite _p_ is the Random Walker (RW), and \(p\rightarrow\infty\) is the Power Watershed (PW), a maximum spanning forest with a small linear solve on each plateau. Reading _p_ as an inverse temperature of the Gibbs distribution over spanning forests, as the probabilistic watershed of Fita Sanmartín et al. [16] suggests (the \(p\rightarrow\infty\) collapse is that of softmax\(\rightarrow\)argmax [24]), every finite-_p_ member is a convex problem whose solution is exactly differentiable, and the path ends at the PW, a true watershed rather than a surrogate as in learned watersheds [32] or post-hoc watershed transforms [5,22].

Our contributions are the following. (i) A differentiable RW/PW layer with unaries, written with dense shifted-grid operators so that it is batched, running on the GPU and can be differentiated in either of two ways: by unrolling a few preconditioned conjugate-gradient steps or implicitly, by one adjoint solve (Sect. 3). Its multi-label form costs one right-hand side per label, and its limit one spanning forest whatever the number of labels, whereas graph cuts are exact only for two labels. (ii) A conditioning study of solver cost, distance to the limit and gradient support as functions of _p_ (Sect. 4.1). (iii) An experimental account on synthetic scenes and PanNuke nuclei [18,17] that evaluates where the WS layer helps. With correct edge costs it recovers exact boundaries; as a binary last layer on real images it is level with a thresholded U-Net; with the instances as labels it is level with a tuned marker watershed on the same network, and ahead of it when training data are scarce (Sect. 4).

## 2 Background and related work

_The_ (_p,q_) _family._ On a graph _G_=(_V,E_) with weights _w<sub>e</sub>\>_0 and seeds \(M\subset V\) with fixed labels, the PW framework [14] minimises

\(E_{p,q}(x)=\sum_{e=\{u,v\}}w_e^p|x_u-x_v|^q.\) (1)

The pair (_p_=1_,q_=1) is the graph cut, (_p_ finite,_q_=2) the RW, and \(p\rightarrow\infty\) the PW, whose solution is unique for _q_=2 and is computed by Kruskal’s algorithm

<tbc>on the edges in decreasing weight, with a _q_-energy minimisation restricted to each plateau of equal weight \[14,27\]. Allène et al. \[2,3\] showed that the min cut of the powered weights becomes a maximum spanning forest cut as _p_ grows, and Cousty et al. \[15\] that this cut is the watershed cut of the graph. Grady’s prior-augmented RW \[20\] adds unary terms, which we use throughout.

#### Learning through segmentation algorithms.

Unrolling an iterative algorithm into a network \[23,26\] and differentiating an optimisation layer implicitly \[4,6\] are well-known techniques; CRF-as-RNN \[33\] unrolls mean-field inference as a last layer. Closest to us, Cerrone et al. \[9\] learn the edge weights of a seeded RW end to end from given seeds; we add unaries, the temperature path to the PW with its exact limit, and instances as labels. Wolf et al. \[32\] learn inside a seeded watershed by structured learning, and spanning structures can also be made differentiable by perturbation \[7\] or stochastic softmax relaxations \[31\]; ours is the deterministic relaxation that the PW framework already contains. In the morphology literature, Challa et al. \[11\] train features with a triplet loss so that a watershed on them classifies hyperspectral pixels, and Chierchia and Perret \[12\] fit ultrametrics, the hierarchical form of the watershed, by gradient descent on a relaxed objective; in both the watershed is differentiated through a surrogate. The deep watershed transform \[5\] and HoVer-Net \[22\] predict maps on which a non-differentiable watershed is run afterwards. Our relaxation is not a surrogate but a member of the same family: the Random Walker is the Power Watershed at finite p, and its limit is the watershed itself.

### 3 The watershed layer

#### 3.1 Energy, temperature and limit

Let \(c_e\ge 0\) be the cost of edge _e_ and, for each pixel _i_, \(c_i^1,c_i^0\ge 0\) the costs of attaching it to the foreground and background labels. With everything raised to the inverse temperature _p_,

\(E_p(x)=\sum_{e=\{u,v\}}w_e\left(x_u-x_v\right)^2+\sum_ia_i^1\left(x_i-1\right)^2+\sum_ia_i^0x_i^2,w_e=e^{-pc_e},a_i^1=e^{-pc_i^1},a_i^0=e^{-pc_i^0}.\text{(2)}\)

Stationarity yields the symmetric positive definite system

\(\left(L(w)+\mathrm{diag}(a^0+a^1)\right)x=a^1,\) (3)

where _L(w_) is the weighted graph Laplacian. The unaries are edges to two virtual label nodes of an augmented graph, so (2) is the seeded (_p,_2) energy on that graph with the two virtual nodes as seeds. Hence _x<sup>p</sup>_ is the probability that a random 2-forest at inverse temperature _p_ connects pixel _i_ to the foreground node (Appendix B.1), and \(x^\infty=\mathrm{lim}_{p\rightarrow\infty} x^p\) is the PW of the augmented graph:

<tbc>a maximum spanning forest flooded from the confident pixels, i.e. a marker- controlled watershed whose markers are decided by the unaries. As the last layer of a network, \(c_i^1=-\alpha logs_i\) and \(c_i^0=-\alpha log(1-s_i)\) with _s_ the network’s soft foreground probability; \(\alpha\) is Grady’s \(\gamma\) and sets how strongly the unaries compete with the edges.

### Many labels.

With _K_ markers (classes or instances), the multi-label RW solves (3) with the shared matrix \(L(w)+\mathrm{diag}(\sum_ka^k)\) and one right-hand side _a<sup>k</sup>_ per label; summing the equations and using _L_**1**=0 shows that the _x<sup>k</sup>_ sum to one, so the output is a per-pixel distribution over this image’s markers. The cost is therefore affine in _K_ and the problem is exact and convex for every _K_. The limit is one spanning forest irrespective of _K_. This is where the family differs most from graph cuts, exact for two labels but NP-hard beyond, where \(\alpha\)-expansion \[8\] is the usual approximation; in the limit the multi-label problem becomes tractable \[3\].

## 3.2 WS layer differentiation

Let _A=L(w_)+diag(_a_<sup>0</sup>+_a_<sup>1</sup>) and let \(\ell(x)\) be the loss. With \(\lambda=A^{-1}\partial\ell/\partial x\) one obtains, for every edge and pixel,

\(\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial w_e}=-(x_u-x_v)(\lambda_u-\lambda_v),\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial a_i^1}=\lambda_i(1-x_i),\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial a_i^0}=-\lambda_ix_i,\) (4)

and the chain rule through _w<sub>e</sub>=e_<sup>-_pc<sub>e</sub>_</sup> contributes a factor -_pw<sub>e</sub>_. This _adjoint solve_ therefore yields the gradient with respect to all costs, with memory independent of the solver’s depth. We term this the _implicit mode_. Alternatively, _T_ steps of Jacobi-preconditioned conjugate gradients are unrolled and differentiated by automatic differentiation. We term this the _unrolled mode_; this is what we deploy when the truncated solver is the WS layer, and _T_ then caps how far a boundary can move, since _T_ iterations propagate information at most in a radius of _T_ pixels. The binary experiments below use the unrolled mode with _T_=20 unless stated; the instance experiments use the implicit mode, solving to a relative residual of 10<sup>-4</sup> (at most 100 iterations) in training and 10<sup>-5</sup> at evaluation, so the radius argument does not restrict them. The two modes do not compute the same thing: at \(p\ge 20\), twenty unrolled steps give the exact gradient of the truncated solver, far from that of the RW (cosine 0.67-0.75 on the edge costs), while the implicit mode matches it to 10<sup>-3</sup> with 30-90 iterations and a constant 0.09GB per batch of 16. On an A100 the multi-marker solve costs 41+20_K_ms per batch of 16 256<sup>2</sup> images with _K_ markers each, and the exact limit 29-51ms per patch on one CPU core for _K_ up to 128 (Appendix F). On a regular grid all operators are dense shifted differences, so the WS layer is batched and can run on a GPU without sparse matrices; the markers of the multi-label form go in the batch dimension. The architectures of the trained models are drawn in Appendix C.The exact limit is evaluated on the CPU by the plateau algorithm of \[14\] with per-label solves on ambiguous plateaus; our implementation agrees with the authors’ reference code to single precision \[1, §B\].

#### Two difficulties.

The limit \(x^\infty\), seen as a function of the weight vector _w_, is locally constant: it changes only when the order of two edge weights flips, which happens on the finitely many hyperplanes where two weights are equal. Away from those ties \(\partial x^\infty/\partial w\) exists and is zero, and on them it is undefined. As _p_ grows, _x<sup>p</sup>_ inherits this behaviour: its gradient is well defined for essentially every weight configuration, but it concentrates on fewer and fewer edges and carries less and less information about which direction would improve the loss. At the same time the solve degrades: \(\lambda_\mathrm{max}(A)\) is at least the largest diagonal entry, hence at least _w_<sub>max</sub>, while \(\lambda_\mathrm{min}(A)\) is at most the weighted degree plus the unary of any pixel (the Rayleigh quotient of its indicator); if some pixel has its four edges at the highest cost, the condition number \(\kappa(A)=\lambda_\mathrm{max}(A)/\lambda_\mathrm{min}(A)\) satisfies \(\kappa(A)\unknown e^{p\Delta c}/4\), with \(\Delta c\) the spread of the edge costs. What matters is therefore \(p\Delta c\), not _p_ alone. With continuous learned costs ties are rare, and the limit reduces to a maximum spanning forest: the plateau solves that distinguish the PW matter only for quantised costs. Section 4.1 measures both these effects.

### 4 Experiments

All code, raw results and the extended version of this article [1] are publicly available<sup>6</sup>. The metrics we use are: intersection over union (IoU), boundary F-score at a pixel tolerance (BF<sub>_t_</sub>), the fraction of pixels with potential in (0.1,0.9) (soft pixels), and, for instance segmentation, F<sub>1</sub> of the matches at IoU 0.5, panoptic quality (PQ) [25], aggregated Jaccard index (AJI) and the relative object-count error. On PanNuke we also report a label-free edge-alignment score, the fraction of predicted boundary pixels within one pixel of a strong colour edge, since the dataset’s semi-automatic contours bound what a boundary score can show. PQ is the product of the segmentation quality SQ, the mean IoU of the matched objects, and the detection quality DQ, an object-level F<sub>1</sub>; it penalises merged and split objects alike.

#### 4.1 The cost of trying to reach the limit

For this experiment, we use three simple images: synthetic shapes with two noise levels \(\sigma\in\{0.05,0.1\}\) and the `camera` image from `scikit-image`. We use hard-seeded RW on \(512\times 512\) 8-bit images with _c<sub>e</sub>_=((_I<sub>u</sub>-I<sub>v</sub>)/_255)<sup>2</sup>. The various seeds are: ground truth eroded by 5 px (edge refinement regime) or 30 px, or only a few scribbles. The reference _x<sup>p</sup>_ is a direct sparse LU solve in double precision with diagonal rescaling and iterative refinement; records whose solve is unreliable are excluded. The limit \(x^\infty\) is computed by the combinatorial PW on the integer costs of the 8-bit image, so that ties, and hence plateaus, are exact.

1 summarizes the results. On the clean image the labels of the limit are reached at _p_≈100 while \(\kappa\) is still low and CG needs only about 50 iterations. This is a comfortable training window, inside which the gradient support has<tbc>

<sup>6</sup> `https://github.com/hugues-talbot/differentiable-power-watershed`

<tbc>already more than halved and beyond which it collapses (7 edges at _p_=1000); support is only a proxy for trainability. Since \(c_e\in[0,1]\) here, _p_ is also \(p\Delta c\); the learned costs of Sects. 4.3-4.4 are trained at \(p\Delta c\lesssim 50\) (costs in \[0,1\] at \(p\le 50\), or a learned scale of 1.85 at _p_=20), inside this window. On noisy and natural images _x<sup>p</sup>_ approaches the limit slowly (a few per cent of the free pixels still differ at _p_=500) while \(\kappa\) goes far beyond what any solver can resolve. The iteration counts grow far more slowly than \(\sqrt{\kappa}\), because the ill-conditioning sits in a few near-isolated pixels that barely affect the residual. The double-precision factorisation itself fails beyond _p_≈500; an exact elimination confirms the table and shows the gap closing slowly beyond (`camera`: 1.2% at \(p=5\cdot 10^3\)), as 8-bit squared costs differ by as little as \(1.5\cdot 10^{-5}\). The last per cent of agreement are out of practical reach of a finite-_p_ solve; they come from the combinatorial step. In the refinement regime 20 unrolled CG steps disagree with the converged solve on 0.04% of the labels (2.9% on the noisy image), independently of the image size; in the global regime (30-px erosion, scribbles) no truncation works.

## 4.2 A tunable, spatially coupled softmax

Fig. 1 shows the WS layer on simulated network outputs. With the image edge on the true boundary and \(\alpha=0.1\), the boundary score BF<sub>2</sub> of the thresholded soft prediction, initially 0.958, becomes 1.000 at _p_=200 and in the limit on the clean scene, and 0.968 at _p_=200 (0.870 in the limit) on the noisy one. The output goes from 22% soft pixels to under 1%: a softmax whose sharpness is spatially coupled through the edges. The scale \(\alpha\) does matter: at \(\alpha=1\) the unaries of confident pixels compete with the noise edges and everything merges before any label attaches, so both large _p_ and the limit collapse. ### 4.3 Real images: a binary last layer

A small U-Net (32-64-128-256 channels) is trained for 30 epochs with Adam on PanNuke [18,17] (nucleus versus background, 256<sup>2</sup>, fold 1 for training, all 2523 patches of fold 2 for testing). Variants: the plain U-Net with binary cross-entropy (BCE), and a U-Net whose logits feed the WS layer as unaries, with edge costs from the image gradient or from a second head of the same network (two more output channels of its last 1\(\times\)1 convolution, through a sigmoid, averaged onto the edges). The WS layer is implemented as 20 unrolled PCG steps with _p_ annealed geometrically from 5 to 50 and the loss BCE on the WS layer output plus 0.5 BCE on the logits. The output of the WS layer is evaluated as trained, converged at the final _p_, and as the exact limit.

2 presents the outcome. A binary WS layer with learned costs is 0.01 IoU and 0.02 BF<sub>2</sub> below a thresholded U-Net in the unrolled mode and level with it in the implicit mode; the same holds on Oxford-IIIT Pet [30], with objects a hundred pixels across [1, §J]. Image-gradient costs are useless on photographs and on cell images alike, as their limit floods whole regions. The exact limit of the learned costs is however deployable at a cost of 0.05 IoU, with a better object-count error than the U-Net. Boundary- and seam-weighted losses, a gap target between touching nuclei, lower annealing ranges and an edge target on the cost head \[1, §L, O\] move these metrics by a few thousandths, with one exception: the edge target, a cross-entropy of the cost maps against the instance boundaries, brings the converged WS layer level with the thresholded U-Net on IoU (paired difference +0.002, 95% bootstrap interval \[-0.000,+0.005\]) and gives the best raw instance scores of the table. Training in the implicit mode, with the true RW gradient (Sect. 3), matters more: on both seeds every paired interval against the unrolled mode is clear of zero (F<sub>1</sub> +0.035 and +0.055), and the layer is level with the U-Net on IoU and BF<sub>2</sub>, 0.007-0.012 behind on F<sub>1</sub> and PQ; the exact limit of these costs is worse (IoU 0.60; Appendix F).

Finally, a U-Net given the same edge supervision through a contour channel, with a marker watershed run on that map afterwards, is level with the edge-target WS layer at the pixel level (last two rows); on raw instance scores the layer is slightly ahead, and after an 8-px minimum-area filter the watershed is.

## 4.4 Real images with labeled instances

The binary WS layer essentially discards the property that makes the PW distinctive. We now let each image carry its own label set, one marker per nucleus plus background, and let the WS layer compute the partition among them (Sect. 3): the U-Net predicts a foreground logit, the edge costs and a marker map; the loss is a per-pixel cross-entropy over this image’s markers against the instance mask, with _p_ annealed from 5 to 20. Each marker region _k_ attaches its pixels to label _k_ with _a<sup>k</sup>=s<sup>p</sup>_ and the background label attaches every pixel with (1-_s)<sup>p</sup>_. The loss is differentiable in the edge costs and the attachments, not in the choice of markers: extraction is a discrete step inside the network, run in training as at test time, and the marker map learns from its own regression loss only. Training markers are first the eroded ground-truth instances. Test markers come from a distance-to-boundary head that regresses, for every nucleus pixel, its normalised distance to the nucleus boundary as in Naylor et al. \[28\]. From<tbc>

3 is where the watershed’s strengths show. With the instances as labels the WS layer raises instance F<sub>1</sub> from 0.656 to 0.795 and PQ from 0.531 to 0.649 over the U-Net with connected components. The last step of that gain comes from training the solve on the model’s own predicted markers, with unmarked nuclei as background in the loss (they still count as misses in every metric). Trained this way the solve _hedges_: through the soft unaries it discounts weak markers and shares contested pixels, so with ground-truth markers it drops 11% of them and its oracle (0.872) falls to the baseline’s (0.867). The fair baseline, the same network and distance head followed by a tuned marker watershed, reaches 0.794 and 0.655. Paired, the WS layer is level on F<sub>1</sub> (+0.001, \[-0.001,+0.004\]), behind on PQ (-0.005, \[-0.008,-0.003\]) and ahead on AJI (+0.009, \[+0.007,+0.012\]); over seeds and fold pairs the two stay within 0.01. They are close for a precise reason: given the WS layer’s own markers and output foreground, a marker watershed on its learned contour map reproduces its partition exactly \[1, §D\]; the two differ through the foreground and the markers only. Nor does the draw depend on the marker head: with a CenterNet-style centre-and-radius detector instead, the WS layer stays at F<sub>1</sub> 0.795 and the watershed baseline drops to 0.774 \[1, §W\]. With a tenth of the training data (266 images, same number of steps) the WS layer leads by 0.015-0.020 F<sub>1</sub> and 0.011-0.015 PQ over three replicates, every paired interval clear of zero: the baseline’s tuning leaves a quarter of the nuclei unmarked, while the hedging solve keeps a permissive threshold and absorbs the spurious markers. From 25% on the baseline is ahead again. The residual PQ gap is the price of the hedging: detections are equal (DQ 0.795 against 0.794) and the hedged boundaries are softer (SQ 0.816 against 0.824). Solved exactly at increasing _p_, the same system traces the path: F<sub>1</sub> peaks at the training _p_=20 and falls monotonically to the limit, which the solve reaches by _p_≈500, while SQ stays at 0.81: a higher _p_ removes the hedging, discounted markers become objects again, and the count error rises from 0.18 to 0.27 (Appendix G). The model trained from true markers is the mirror image, within 0.006 F<sub>1</sub> of its limit but behind on its own markers ( 3): a deployable limit and tolerance to imperfect markers pulled in opposite directions in every schedule we tried.

## 5 Conclusion

The Random Walker at finite _p_ gives the Power Watershed a differentiable form that is exact rather than a surrogate: every _p_ yields a convex problem differentiated through one adjoint solve, the multi-label problem is exact at a cost affine in the number of labels and as \(p\rightarrow\infty\) the solution converges to that of the combinatorial algorithm. A conditioning study shows what this path costs: the solve and the gradient both degrade as _p_ grows, so training happens<tbc>

## A Questions a reader may ask

The main text had to be short. This section answers, in order, the questions that the authors and their reviewers asked while writing it, with pointers to where the evidence is.

### What is the WS layer, in one sentence?

A seeded Random Walker at a finite inverse temperature _p_, with unaries, whose edge costs and unaries are produced by the network, trained through, and whose \(p\rightarrow\infty\) limit is the Power Watershed of the same costs. At the temperature it is trained at, its partition between markers is a marker watershed of its learned contour map (Appendix D,  5: identical to three digits on 2523 patches). The finite temperature adds one thing a watershed does not have: the solve can hedge, i.e. discount a weak marker through the soft unaries and share contested pixels between neighbours.

### A post-hoc marker watershed also turns a U-Net into an instance segmenter with any number of labels.

_What is new?_ Where the partition happens. In HoVer- Net-style pipelines the watershed runs after training, on maps the network was trained to predict; the loss never sees the partition. In the WS layer the partition over a per-image label set is a layer of the network, and the cross-entropy over that label set trains the edge costs, the foreground and the marker attachments through the solve (Sect. 4.4). Two properties of the (_p,q_) family make this cheap: the Random Walker’s cost is affine in the number of labels (one shared matrix, one right-hand side per label), and the limit is one spanning forest whatever that number (Sect. 3), where graph cuts are exact for two labels only. The number of labels is set per image by the markers, not by the output layout. The markers themselves remain a discrete step; see below.

### The baseline’s watershed is "tuned".

_Does that mean a second training?_ No: a grid search over a few scalars on 300 patches of a held-out fold (fold 3, used neither for training nor for testing), scored by PQ, five minutes in all. The baseline has four choices (marker threshold, minimum marker area, prominence of the distance maxima, and the relief: the contour map, the negative distance map or their sum; 135 settings). The WS layer’s marker extraction is chosen the same way with the first three (72 settings); its _p_ schedule is fixed. So the honest contrast is not "end to end versus tuned": both pipelines tune how markers are read off the distance map; only the baseline also tunes the assignment step, which the WS layer learns (Appendix D). The tuning stage is where the baseline is brittle: at a tenth of the training data its grid search picks a high marker threshold and leaves a quarter of the nuclei unmarked, while the WS layer keeps a permissive threshold at every data size because its trained solve absorbs the spurious markers (Appendix E).

### "The same network": is the baseline’s U-Net trained the same way?

Same architecture, same three output heads, same targets and training recipe, without the solve in the loop. The baseline U-Net predicts a foreground logit (cross-entropy against the binary nucleus mask), a two-channel contour map (the edge target:

<tbc>a cross-entropy against the grid edges where the instance label changes, seams between touching nuclei weighted up) and a distance map (the normalised distance of each nucleus pixel to its boundary, squared error, as in HoVer-Net’s distance variant), trained on fold 1 for 30 epochs with the same optimiser, batch size and augmentation. The WS-layer model predicts the same four channels with the same three losses, the contour map becoming the edge costs through a sigmoid and a learned scale, plus the partition cross-entropy over the markers, which reaches the foreground logit and the costs through the solve; its foreground loss is an auxiliary term at half weight. So the heads differ in one respect after training: the baseline’s foreground head is trained only to be a mask and is the best of the study (IoU 0.725 thresholded), while the layer’s foreground head degenerates to speckle, since the solve needs it only as a soft prior, and the layer’s output foreground stays 0.01 IoU below. The distance heads come out equivalent. Both pipelines then read markers off their distance maps by the same rule, and the baseline floods a watershed from them inside its thresholded foreground (Appendix D).

## Why does the WS layer only match the tuned watershed at full data?

Because, given the same markers and the same foreground, the two compute the same partition ( 5), and the remaining errors are in marker detection, which both share: with ground-truth markers both reach _F_<sub>1</sub> about 0.87 ( 3). Every advantage the WS layer showed during the study was matched once the baseline received the same supervision: the edge target (Sect. 4.3, last rows of  2) and the distance head (Sect. 4.4). Changing the marker head does not change this: with a CenterNet-style centre-and-radius detector the WS layer stays at _F_<sub>1</sub> 0.795 and the baseline drops to 0.774 (record section "A detection head for the markers").

## Why did the oracle with true markers fall from 0.96 to 0.87?

Because of the hedging. Trained from ground-truth markers, the costs could trust every marker and the marker attachment overrode the foreground (oracle 0.959). Trained from the model’s own markers, the solve learns to veto a marker where the foreground is weak and to share contested pixels; with ground-truth markers it then drops 11% of them, and its oracle (0.872) falls to the watershed’s (0.867). The 0.17 _F_<sub>1</sub> between the earlier layer and its oracle was therefore a property of training on perfect markers, not headroom (record section "Training the solve from the model’s own markers"). The same hedging explains the layer’s PQ deficit (softer boundaries at equal detection, SQ 0.816 against 0.824) and its loss at the exact limit, which removes the hedging.

## Why can the marker selection not be learned through the layer?

Because the partition loss reaches a marker only through the pixels it claims. A spurious marker where the background is clearly stronger claims no pixels at any strength, so its strength receives no gradient (measured at 10<sup>-11</sup>) and is never pushed down; a true marker whose region spills over the nucleus rim loses rim pixels, so its strength is pushed down. The strengths therefore learn a rim correction, not<tbc>

<tbc>a ranking: the learned strength ranks background candidates above true nuclei (AUC 0.11–0.13). Three designs were tried, strengths from the marker head’s own score (which also degraded the head as a detector, _F_<sub>1</sub> 0.732), a fifth output channel, and a detached scorer on candidate features, and none beat the same recipe with all strengths fixed at one (record sections "Marker selection in the gradient path" and "Selection without touching the marker head"). Detection confidences from a detection head used as fixed strengths do not help either (record section "A detection head for the markers"). Marker detection is a different question from pixel partition, and the gradient through the partition does not answer it.

## Is the exact limit the deployed object?

Not in these experiments. On the instance model, solved exactly at increasing _p_ with costs and markers fixed, accuracy peaks at the training _p_=20 and falls monotonically to the limit (0.795 to 0.724 _F_<sub>1</sub>), which the solve reaches by _p_≈500 (Appendix G). What a higher _p_ removes is the hedging: discounted markers become objects again. The model trained from true markers is the mirror image: within 0.006 _F_<sub>1</sub> of its limit, but worse on its own markers. A deployable limit and tolerance to imperfect markers pulled in opposite directions in every schedule tried. For the binary models the picture differs: pixel IoU is flat up to the training _p_ and then loses 0.05 at the limit, while instance _F_<sub>1</sub> keeps rising to _p_≈200, because a high _p_ removes the faint blobs that thresholding a soft output leaves ( 9 and the record section "Accuracy against _p_").

## Is there a training regime that lets the combinatorial watershed replace the WS layer at inference?

Partly, and the record says what it needs. Two trained models already have a deployable limit: the binary layer with the edge target trained at _p_ from 5 to 50 (limit 0.016 IoU below the converged solve, no loss on BF<sub>2</sub>; Sect. 4.3) and the multi-marker layer trained from ground-truth markers at _p_ from 5 to 20 (limit 0.006 _F_<sub>1</sub> below the solve on all of fold 2;  3 and the record section "The exact limit on all of fold 2"). What they share, and what the models with a lost limit lack: costs trained to cut between every pair of neighbouring markers with the background as a soft seed, which is what a maximum spanning forest needs (the binary models trained at low _p_ lost their limit entirely); sharp contours from the edge target, which cut the limit’s price from 0.046 to 0.016 IoU; and no hedging, since training from the model’s own markers or in the implicit mode makes the costs rely on finite-_p_ softness that the limit removes. Those last two are exactly our best finite-_p_ models, so the trade-off stated in the main text is the obstacle: the tolerance to imperfect markers lives in the softness, and the limit has none. A regime for the combinatorial watershed must move that tolerance out of the solve and into the marker rule. Four candidates, none run, cheapest first: (i) re-tune the marker thresholds for the limit’s output on the tuning fold, since the limit rows reuse thresholds tuned for the solve, which are permissive because the solve absorbs spurious markers and the limit cannot (a grid search at 50ms per patch, no training; we expect it to recover most of the 0.07 _F_<sub>1</sub>, leaving a watershed on learned costs with its own tuned markers, i.e.

<tbc>about the baseline’s score); (ii) straight-through training, the exact limit in the forward pass and the Random Walker adjoint at moderate _p_ in the backward pass, so that the loss sees the deployed partition, hedging cannot be learned, and the gradient is the relaxation’s, which  5 suggests points the right way; (iii) a high-_p_ phase at the end of the schedule, limited by the solver (PCG stops converging beyond _p_≈50 on these costs, the exact elimination of Appendix G takes about 2s per patch on one core, enough for a few fine-tuning epochs); (iv) a margin loss on the ordering of the edge weights, which is all the limit depends on, i.e. the learned-watershed route of Wolf et al. with our path as a warm start. None of these would make the limit better than the finite-_p_ solve on PanNuke, since the solve’s advantage is the hedging itself; they would make "train at finite _p_, deploy at the limit" a single consistent procedure.

_What is the "diagonal rescaling" of the reference solve, and is it an estimate of the largest eigenvalue?_ No; the two uses of the diagonal are different. The reference solve of Sect. 4.1 factorises the Jacobi-scaled matrix _SAS_ with _S_=diag(_A_)<sup>-1/2</sup>, so that every diagonal entry of the scaled matrix is one, solves, maps back with _S_, and then runs two steps of iterative refinement on the original system. It is needed because at large _p_ the diagonal entries of _A_ are sums of weights _e_<sup>-_pc_</sup> that span many orders of magnitude from one pixel to the next, and a sparse LU of the raw matrix loses its pivots to underflow or cancellation; scaling each row and column by the inverse square root of its diagonal equalises the magnitudes, and it is the near-optimal diagonal scaling for the condition number (van der Sluis). The largest diagonal entry appears instead in the bound of Sect. 3: for a symmetric positive definite matrix, \(\lambda_\mathrm{max}\) is at least every diagonal entry (the Rayleigh quotient of a unit vector), which with the upper bound on \(\lambda_\mathrm{min}\) from a pixel whose four edges carry the highest cost gives \(\kappa(A)\unknown e^{p\Delta c}/4\). So the diagonal bounds the condition number in one place and improves it in the other.

_Why does the binary WS layer not beat a thresholded U-Net?_ Because a U-Net trained with cross-entropy for 30 epochs learns a similar sharpening by itself. Inside the trained model the layer does what it should (its own logits are speckle, 350 components per patch, which the layer cleans up to the true 24), but the two- stage system is not better than the one-stage one, on Pet or on PanNuke, under a plain cross-entropy or under boundary-weighted, seam-weighted or Dice-band losses (the record’s Pet and PanNuke binary sections). Two things did matter: an edge target on the cost head (Sect. 4.3) and training in the implicit mode, i.e. with the true Random Walker gradient, which lifts the binary layer to the U-Net’s pixel scores (Appendix F). Twenty unrolled conjugate-gradient steps give the exact gradient of the truncated solver, not of the Random Walker, at \(p\ge 20\).

_So what does training through the watershed buy?_ Three things the experiments support: the assignment step is learned rather than tuned, so the pipeline has no post-hoc choice of relief or threshold on the partition; the trained solve tolerates imperfect markers, which shows as the lead when annotations are scarce and as the best count error of the study; and the whole model is one differentiable<tbc>

<tbc>module with a cost affine in the number of labels, so losses defined on the partition (and, in future work, weak or scribble supervision) can reach the costs. What it does not buy on PanNuke is accuracy beyond a well-tuned post-hoc watershed with the same supervision, and the paper says so.

## B Derivations

### B.1 Random walks and random forests

Grady reads the seeded Random Walker as follows: _x<sub>i</sub>_ is the probability that a random walk started at pixel _i_, which crosses edge _e_ with probability proportional to _w<sub>e</sub>_, reaches a foreground seed before a background seed. Sect. 3 reads the same _x<sub>i</sub>_ as the probability that a random 2-forest connects _i_ to the foreground node. The two readings are the same harmonic function, written in two ways; the forest reading is the probabilistic watershed of Fita Sanmartín et al. \[16\], restated here on the augmented graph, where the unaries are edges to the label nodes.

Let \(G'\) be the augmented graph: the pixel graph, two label nodes _F_ and _B_, and for every pixel _i_ the edges (_i,F_) of weight \(a_i^1\) and (_i,B_) of weight \(a_i^0\). Let \(L'\) be its Laplacian and \(L'_U\) the submatrix on the pixels, i.e. \(L'\) with the rows and columns of _F_ and _B_ removed, so that \(L'_U=L(w)+\text{diag}(a^0+a^1)\) and system (3) reads \(L'_UX=a^1\).

_Random walk._ Let _h<sub>i</sub>_ be the probability that the walk from _i_ reaches _F_ before _B_. Then _h<sub>F</sub>_=1, _h<sub>B</sub>_=0, and at every pixel the first step gives \(h_i=\sum_{j\sim i}w_{ij}h_j/\sum_{j\sim i}w_{ij}\), the sum running over the pixel neighbours and the two label nodes. This says \((L'h)_i=0\) at every pixel with the boundary values on _F_ and _B_, i.e. \(L'_Uh=a^1\). The system is non-singular (it is diagonally dominant with a strictly dominant row wherever a unary is positive), so _h=x_.

_Random 2-forest._ By Cramer’s rule, \(x_i=\text{det}L'_U[i\leftarrow a^1]/\text{det}L'_U\), where \([i\leftarrow a^1]\) replaces column _i_ by the right-hand side. The all-minors matrix-tree theorem \[10\] evaluates both determinants. \(\text{det}L'_U\) is the minor of \(L'\) with the vertices _F_ and _B_ deleted: it equals the sum, over the spanning forests of \(G'\) with exactly two trees, one containing _F_ and the other _B_, of the product of the edge weights of the forest. The numerator is, up to a sign that cancels in the ratio, the minor of \(L'\) with rows {_F,B_} and columns {_i,B_} deleted, which the same theorem evaluates as the sum over those 2-forests in which _i_ lies in the tree of _F_. Hence

\(x_i=\frac{\sum_{\mathcal{F}:i\sim F}\prod_{e\in\mathcal{F}}w_e}{\sum_\mathcal{F}\prod_{e\in\mathcal{F}}w_e},\) (5)

the probability that _i_ is attached to _F_ when a 2-forest is drawn with probability proportional to its weight. With _w<sub>e</sub>=e_<sup>-_pc<sub>e</sub>_</sup> and _a=e_<sup>-_pc_</sup> the weight of a forest is \(e^{-p}\sum_{e\in\mathcal{F}}c_e\): the distribution is the Gibbs distribution over 2-forests with energy the total cost of the forest, at inverse temperature _p_. As \(p\rightarrow\infty\) it concentrates on the forests of minimum total cost, i.e. on the maximum-weight spanning forests separating _F_ from _B_, which is the Power Watershed; when several forests tie,

the measure is uniform over them, and that uniform average is what the plateau solve of the PW algorithm computes.

With _K_ labels the same theorem, applied with the _K_+1 label nodes as the deleted set, gives \(x_i^k\) as the probability that _i_ lies in the tree of label _k_ when a (_K_+1)-forest, each tree containing exactly one label node, is drawn with probability proportional to its weight. Since every pixel lies in exactly one tree, the \(x_i^k\) sum to one, which is the combinatorial form of Appendix B.3.

### B.2 The adjoint gradient

Take \(E(x,w)=\sum_{e=\{u,v\}}w_e(x_u-x_v)^2+\sum_ia_i^1(x_i-1)^2+\sum_ia_i^0x_i^2\). Stationarity gives _Ax=a_<sup>1</sup> with _A=L(w_)+diag(_a_<sup>0</sup>+_a_<sup>1</sup>). Differentiating with respect to one parameter \(\theta\), \(A\partial x/\partial\theta=\partial a^1/\partial\theta-(\partial A/\partial\theta)x\), so for a loss \(\ell(x)\) and \(\lambda=A^{-1}\partial\ell/\partial x\) (using the symmetry of _A_), \(\partial\ell/\partial\theta=\lambda^\top(\partial a^1/\partial\theta-(\partial A/\partial\theta)x)\). For \(\theta=w_e\), \(\partial A/\partial w_e\) is the elementary edge Laplacian, whose product with _x_ has entries _x<sub>u</sub>-x<sub>v</sub>_ at _u_ and _x<sub>v</sub>-x<sub>u</sub>_ at _v_, giving \(\partial\ell/\partial w_e=-(x_u-x_v)(\lambda_u-\lambda_v)\). For \(\theta=a_i^1\), \(\partial a^1/\partial a_i^1=e_i\) and \((\partial A/\partial a_i^1)x=x_ie_i\), giving \(\lambda_i(1-x_i)\); for \(\theta=a_i^0\) only the second term survives, giving \(-\lambda_ix_i\). The chain rule through _w<sub>e</sub>=e_<sup>-_pc<sub>e</sub>_</sup> contributes -_pw<sub>e</sub>_, whose growth in _p_ is the algebraic counterpart of the conditioning blow-up.

### B.3 Multi-label solutions sum to one

With _K_ labels, \(A_K=L(w)+\mathrm{diag}(\sum_ka^k)\) and _A<sub>K</sub>x<sup>k</sup>=a<sup>k</sup>_. Summing over _k_, \(A_K\sum_kx^k=\sum_ka^k=A_K\mathbf{1}\) since _L_**1**=0; _A<sub>K</sub>_ is positive definite, hence \(\sum_kx^k=\mathbf{1}\).

### B.4 The exact limit with _K_ labels

The plateau algorithm of Couprie et al. processes the edges by decreasing weight and merges the nodes of a plateau unless the plateau connects nodes with two or more distinct known labels, in which case the _q_=2 energy is minimised on the plateau with the known nodes as boundary. For two labels the boundary values are scalars; for _K_ labels we solve one system per label with one-hot boundary values and assign the argmax, which is the limit of the multi-label RW on the plateau. Singleton plateaus (continuous costs) are processed by a scalar union- find; plateaus of at most 64 edges by a pure-Python union-find; larger plateaus by the vectorised path.

### B.5 Fixed-point reweighting

The following variant of the WS layer is studied in the experimental record below (sections on reweighting) but is not used in the instance pipeline of the main text.

<tbc>Instead of raising the weights to a growing _p_, one can keep a benign base _p_<sub>0</sub> and iterate, multiplying each weight by a factor of the current solution,

\(w_e\leftarrow w_e^0\rho(x_u-x_v),a_i^1\leftarrow a_i^{1,0}\rho(x_i-1),a_i^0\leftarrow a_i^{0,0}\rho(x_i),\rho(d)=\frac{\varepsilon^2}{\varepsilon^2+d^2},\) (6)

and re-solving (3) until the pair (weights, solution) stops changing. This is the half-quadratic / majorise-minimise iteration of a nonconvex piecewise-constant energy with the Geman-McClure potential [19,29]; the unaries are reweighted too because they are edges of the augmented graph. The weights stay in (0,1] and the smallest factor is set by \(\varepsilon\), not by _p_ times the cost spread, and the tiny weights appear only on the edges across which the solution jumps. The fixed point is not the PW: it is a local minimiser that depends on the starting point, which for a finishing layer is the network’s own prediction. Inner solves are implicit and the outer loop is differentiated by automatic differentiation (checked against finite differences).

### B.6 Validation against the reference implementation

Our NumPy implementation of the plateau algorithm was checked against the authors’ reference code (PW\_1.0.1, `https://sourceforge.net/projects/ powerwatershed`) on the same 4-connected graphs, integer weights and seeds: on 80 random coarsely quantised images with two to five labels and on thirteen 512<sup>2</sup> cases (synthetic, camera, astronaut; two- and multi-label) the potentials agree to single precision (maximum difference \(6\cdot 10^{-8}\), the reference stores them as float) and the labels agree on every pixel once the same rule is applied to potentials exactly equal to 0.5. The reference realises the plateaus of the merged graph through a geodesic reconstruction of the weights from the seeds; without it, its result depends on the order in which equal weights are sorted. The harness and the records are in the code repository (`experiments/pwref/`, `results/pwref/`).

## What is shared.

Both models are the same U-Net (32-64-128-256 channels) with a four-channel last layer, trained with the same recipe: fold 1, 30 epochs, batch 16, the eight flips and rotations as augmentation, Adam with learning rate 10<sup>-3</sup> and cosine decay, one seed. The four channels and their direct supervision are identical:

- channel 0, the foreground logit, whose sigmoid _s_ is trained with a binary cross-entropy against the nucleus mask;<tbc>

**-** channels 1-2, the contour (or edge-cost) head, trained against the map of instance boundaries derived from the instance masks (the edge target of Sect. 4.3), seams between touching nuclei weighted five times;<tbc>

**-** channel 3, the distance head of Naylor et al. [28]: for every nucleus pixel the Chebyshev distance to the nucleus boundary, capped at 12 px and divided by the nucleus’s maximum, so that every nucleus peaks at 1; sigmoid output, squared error.

Test markers are extracted from the predicted distance map _d_ by the same procedure for both models:

1. seeds are the regional maxima of _d_ of prominence at least _h_ (the _h_-maxima), kept where _d\>t_, one seed per plateau;<tbc>

2. each seed is grown into a basin by a watershed of -_d_ inside {_d\>t_}, so that two touching nuclei whose maxima are separated by a valley deeper than _h_ get two markers even when the valley stays above _t_;<tbc>

3. basins smaller than _a_ pixels are dropped.

The result is a label map with one connected marker region per detected nucleus. The three parameters are chosen separately for each model by the panoptic quality of its final output on 300 evenly spaced patches of fold 3, which is used neither for training nor for testing. Both procedures are therefore identical; the markers are not, because each model predicts its own _d_ and has its own tuned parameters ( 4).

## The baseline’s final step.

A marker watershed (4-connected) of a relief _r_ from the markers, inside the foreground mask {_s\>_0.5}; foreground components that contain no marker are left unlabelled. The relief is chosen on fold 3 among the contour map _c_ (mean of the two contour channels), -_d_, and _c-d_; the choice hardly matters (PQ 0.654-0.655 on fold 2 for the three). This is the post-processing of HoVer-Net [22] applied to Naylor et al.’s distance map; it receives no gradient. Keeping the unmarked foreground components as extra instances lowers F<sub>1</sub> to 0.780 and PQ to 0.637 and raises AJI to 0.666, so they are dropped.

## The WS layer’s final step.

The multi-marker Random Walker of Sect. 3 at the final temperature _p_=20, solved to convergence: every marker region _k_ attaches its pixels to label _k_ with the unary _a<sup>k</sup>=s<sup>p</sup>_, the background label attaches every pixel with (1-_s)<sup>p</sup>_ (the costs -log_s_ and -log(1-_s_) clipped at 8), the edge weights are _e_<sup>-_pc<sub>e</sub>_</sup> with _c<sub>e</sub>_ the edge costs of channels 1-2 (times a learned scale),

<tbc>and every pixel takes the label of its largest probability _x<sup>k</sup>_. During training the same solve is differentiated, the loss being the per-pixel cross-entropy of the label probabilities against the instance map (seam pixels weighted six times), added to the three direct losses above; _p_ is annealed from 5 to 20. The training markers are the ground-truth nuclei eroded by 2-3 px for the first ten epochs, then a mix, and the model’s own extracted markers from epoch 15; nuclei that receive no marker are given to the background label in the loss, as they would be at test time. The extraction is thus inside the training loop but outside the gradient: the solve’s gradient reaches the edge-cost channels through _w_ and the foreground channel through the unaries _a<sup>k</sup>=s<sup>p</sup>_ and _a_<sup>0</sup>=(1-_s)<sup>p</sup>_, never the distance channel, which learns only from its own squared error. A variant that puts the selection in the gradient path (every regional maximum above _t_=0.1 a candidate, with a strength \(\sigma_k\) computed from the mean distance logit over the candidate by a sigmoid with learned offset and temperature, entering as \(a^k=(\sigma_ks)^p\), duplicates and background candidates pushed towards zero strength by the cross-entropy) lost 0.063 F<sub>1</sub> and 0.048 PQ against this recipe on fold 2: the strengths barely separated true from spurious candidates, and the gradient reaching the distance channel doubled the share of unmarked nuclei (26% against 12.7%; extended report, Sect. 14).

The baseline’s tuning picks a high threshold: it misses a fifth of the nuclei but keeps spurious markers rare, because its watershed turns every marker inside the foreground into an object. The WS layer’s tuning picks a low one: it detects more nuclei and lets its solve, trained on such markers, absorb the spurious ones. An extended grid (_t_ from 0.4 to 0.7) gives the baseline the same choice; the WS layer’s _t_=0.2 is the lowest value of its grid, and for the earlier distance-head model of the record an extended grid down to _t_=0.1 still chose 0.2.

### Gradient accuracy.

We compare, on eight fold-2 patches and the binary WS layer with learned costs (Sect. 4.3), the gradient of the binary cross-entropy with respect to the edge costs and to the unaries against a reference: automatic differentiation through a double-precision PCG run to a relative residual of 10<sup>-12</sup>. Central finite differences on the converged solve agree with that reference to a median relative error below 10<sup>-8</sup>. Figure 7 gives the median relative error. The unrolled mode computes the exact gradient of the _truncated_ solver, as its double-precision curve shows, but that is not the gradient of the RW. At _p_=5, _T_=20 steps are already close (cosine 0.993); at _p_=20 and _p_=50 the same 20 steps leave a relative error of 0.9 (cosine 0.75 and 0.67), and _T_=50 and _T_=200 respectively are needed to fall below 5%. The implicit mode at the training tolerance (10<sup>-4</sup>, at most 100 iterations) stays within \(1.6\cdot 10^{-3}\) at every _p_, with 30, 62 and 92 forward iterations at _p_=5, 20 and 50 and as many adjoint ones.

### Time and memory, binary layer.

In time, forward plus backward, the implicit mode at _p_=20 costs as much as about 45 unrolled steps, at _p_=50 as much as about 65.

The Jacobi-PCG used in training is accurate only near the training _p_: on 256 patches it matches the exact solve to 0.015% of the pixels at \(p\le 20\), differs on 0.5% at _p_=35, and from _p_=100 reaches its iteration cap in single and double precision with 5-12% of the pixels wrong. The sweep therefore uses an elimination free of subtractions (the GTH variant of Gaussian elimination, in the log domain), about 2s per patch at any _p_; its outputs sum to one within 10<sup>-13</sup>, and it agrees with sparse LU on 32 patches at \(p\le 100\) and with the training solver at \(p\le 20\).

Accuracy rises up to the training _p_ and then falls monotonically towards the limit, which the curve reaches by _p_≈500; most of the 0.07 F<sub>1</sub> and 0.06 PQ gap has opened by _p_=100. The quality of the matched nuclei (SQ) stays between 0.809 and 0.816 from _p_=20 on, so the loss is in detection. The fraction of pixels labelled unlike the limit decreases steadily; on three patches it is zero at _p_=3000, direct evidence that the finite-_p_ solve tends to our exact limit on the same costs.

- Natural images are the hard case. The PW limit of a raw-gradient graph on a photograph is simply far from any finite-p solution, which is the same message as the Pets results below: on photographs the edge costs have to be learned.<tbc>

33<tbc>

<tbc>reaches the limit’s labels at p = 100 for 53 CG iterations, \(|\Delta\text{I}|\) at p = 50 for 115, the rank at p = 50 for 259. On the natural image the rank and \(|\Delta\text{I}|\) get closer to the limit than the squared cost ever does (1-2 % of the free pixels at p = 100-200 against 4 % at p = 500) for about twice the iterations, but with the float64 reference already failing there. What the transforms do change is where the gradient dies: with the rank, 90 % of the gradient mass sits on 20 edges by p = 50, at the very p where the limit is first reached, while with the squared cost 6 000 edges still carry it at the corresponding point. So for annealing, the squared cost, which spends the dynamic range on the strong edges, is the better path: the limit is reached while the gradient is still alive. The rank normalisation keeps its other role, fixing the output distribution of a learned cost head so that p means the same thing on every image.

# The Power Watershed as a Differentiable Layer

37<tbc>

<tbc>`rw\_learned` model, layer minus its own logits: +0.035 IoU, +0.068 BF<sub>2</sub>, better on 81 % / 86 % of the patches. Limit minus converged on the same 307 patches: -0.046 IoU [-0.066, -0.027], -0.034 BF<sub>2</sub>.

Figures: `results/pannuke/figures/training.png`,`examples\_\<variant\>.png` (full patches) and `examples\_\<variant\>\_crop.png` (64-px crops around the densest cluster of touching nuclei), for the 8 fold-2 patches with the most touching- nuclei pixels; all eight are Colon, where crowding is worst.

- **Honest outcome: on real nuclei the WS layer does not help, and costs a little.** The learned-cost variant is 0.01 IoU and 0.017 BF<sub>2</sub> below the plain U-Net, consistently across tolerances (1, 2, 3 px), tissues (HeadNeck is the one exception, +0.02 IoU and +0.014 BF<sub>2</sub> on 169 patches), and at the instance level (F1 0.60 vs 0.66, PQ 0.48 vs 0.53). The difference is small but not noise. The image-gradient variant is clearly worse, as on Pets.<tbc>

- **Why: the WS layer is a smoother here, and nuclei are small.** With p \(\le\) 50 the WS layer diffuses the unaries across every edge whose cost is not large, so the output is softer than the U-Net’s (16 % soft pixels against 15 %, and visibly blurrier blobs in `examples\_rw\_learned\_crop.png`), and it bridges the 1-2 px gaps between touching nuclei that the U-Net’s logits keep. On Pets the object was 100 px across and this cost nothing; on nuclei about 25 px across it costs the boundary metrics directly and the instance count indirectly (the IoU gap grows with the number of nuclei per patch). The learned edge head is nevertheless a clean contour detector that does respond to the interfaces between touching nuclei (last column of the crop panels), but its contours are 2-3 px wide and the costs along them are not large enough at p = 50 to stop the diffusion. Lower p than Pets was never tried, nor a sharper cost parametrisation (e.g. the costs through an exponential rather than a sigmoid).<tbc>

- **The division of labour is extreme.** As on Pets, the network leaves the decision to the WS layer: its own logits are a checkerboard of speckle (348 components per patch against 24 true nuclei, F1 0.08) that the WS layer cleans up into 23.8 components with F1 0.60. The WS layer adds 0.035 IoU and 0.068 BF<sub>2</sub> over its own logits, but the two-stage system does not beat the one-stage one.<tbc>

**-** **Deployment at p** \(=\infty\) **costs 0.05 IoU at the pixel level but is the best instance segmenter of the RW outputs.** The exact PW limit on the learned costs loses 0.046 IoU and 0.034 BF<sub>2</sub> against the converged finite-p solve, and the panels show why: in crowded regions it floods whole clusters into one component. Yet on the same 307 patches its instance metrics are better than the WS layer’s (F1 0.618 vs 0.581, PQ 0.49 vs 0.46, count error 0.25 vs 0.34), because it is binary and removes the faint spurious blobs that survive thresholding the soft output; on Breast it even reaches the U-Net’s PQ (0.535 vs 0.547) with a lower count error. The train-at-finite-p / deploy- at-the-limit scheme therefore works on real data in the sense that the limit is usable (unlike with image-gradient costs, 0.18 IoU), but it is not free.

**- The label-noise caveat, measured.** The ground-truth boundaries lie within 1 px of a strong colour edge only 55.9 % of the time; every method’s output does so at least as often (U-Net 57.7 %, layer 57.9 %, limit 57.7 %). Either the labels are indeed a pixel or two off the visible edge, or nucleus boundaries on H&E are often not strong colour edges at all (cytoplasm and nucleus of similar hue). In both cases boundary F-scores at 1 px against these labels cannot separate a method that follows the image from one that follows the label noise, which is part of the reason the BF<sub>1</sub> gap (-0.023) is larger than the BF<sub>3</sub> gap (-0.012). The `rw\_img` limit shows the other side: it follows image edges 80 % of the time and is useless. A dataset with pixel-accurate manual boundaries (CoNSeP, MoNuSeg) is needed for the pixel-level boundary claim; the instance metrics above do not depend on the exact boundary and already tell the same story.<tbc>

**- **What the WS layer would need to help here.** Edge costs that are sharp and large where nuclei touch (a cost head trained with an explicit boundary target, or costs from the instance interfaces that the data provide), a target that leaves the interface pixels as background so that separating nuclei is rewarded, and a lower p, or a p-dependent cost scale, so that the WS layer stops being a smoother before it is a cutter. Section 6.1 tries the target, the lower p and the sharper parametrisation.

What is left untried, and would be needed before concluding that a cut-capable last layer cannot help on nuclei: supervising the cost head directly with the seam mask (an edge target rather than hoping the segmentation loss finds it), a loss that pays for the separation of instances rather than for pixels near seams, and a dataset with pixel-accurate boundaries where a 1-px seam is a real image feature.

The same filter is applied to every row of the second table, so the ranking it gives is fair: boundary loss \> instance loss \> BCE for the U-Net, and the WS layer 0.03-0.08 F1 below the U-Net under each. The filter also corrects one reading of section 6: with it, the BCE layer (F1 0.633) is above its own exact limit (0.618), so the limit’s raw instance advantage there was partly that it carries no faint blobs to begin with; its count error (0.246 vs 0.268) remains the best of the RW outputs under BCE.<tbc>

- **The instance loss did not teach either model to separate nuclei.** The seam is 0.09 % of the pixels; even at \(\times\)21 it is 2 % of the loss, and the U-Net’s output is indistinguishable from its BCE output at the pixel level (paired differences within \(\pm\)0.002), with a marginal instance gain (F1 0.663 vs 0.656 raw, 0.696 vs 0.683 filtered) and more spurious small components (count error 0.315 vs 0.275 raw). For the WS layer the effect was negative on everything: 0.01 IoU below its BCE self, 18 % soft pixels, and the learned edge head stopped being a contour detector: under this loss its costs are diffuse blobs inside the nuclei rather than lines along their boundaries (last column of `instance/figures/examples\_rw\_learned\_crop.png`), so the exact limit floods whole clusters (0.59 IoU, -0.108 against the converged solve). Asking the WS layer to put a 2-px background seam between two touching nuclei at p \(\le\) 50 is asking a diffusion to produce a line; the cost head would need a cost of order cmax across the seam and nothing elsewhere, and the gradient through 20 PCG steps did not find that solution. A seam loss on the cost head directly (an edge target), rather than on the WS layer output, is the obvious next thing to try, and was not tried here.<tbc>

- **Where the limit stands.** Under the boundary loss the exact PW limit improves on its BCE self (0.673 vs 0.661 IoU, 0.755 vs 0.711 BF<sub>2</sub>) and its price against the converged solve drops from 0.046 to 0.034 IoU and from 0.034 to 0.013 BF<sub>2</sub>, i.e. the sharper the trained solution, the less the limit loses. ## M Fixed-point reweighting instead of exponentiation

This is the half-quadratic / majorize-minimize reweighting of the \(\ell 0\) project applied inside the WS layer. Implementation: `RWLLayer(mode="reweighted")` in `experiments/pw\_layer.py`; base weights exp(-p<sub>0</sub> c), then `outer`=5 steps of

**– **The fixed point is rigid.** At the fixed point the losing unary of every pixel is down-weighted by \(\varepsilon^2\), so each pixel is locked to its label and the output’s sensitivity to the edge costs collapses onto 70-140 edges on the noisy scene, against 4000 for the annealed solution of the same quality; on the clean scene the two are comparable (1300 vs 1200-4000). This is the self-reinforcing nature of the scheme, the same thing that makes it sharp, and it is the price of losing the temperature: for training, the gradient should be taken after one or two reweighting steps or with a larger \(\varepsilon\), i.e. at finite temperature again, with the fully converged fixed point used only at deployment. Note that the ground-truth loss gradient is not the right measure here: it shrinks whenever the output is right.<tbc>

**– **Same failure mode, gentler.** With the image edge off the true boundary, the fixed point from p<sub>0</sub> = 10 degrades gracefully (0.87-0.89 against 0.96) because it sharpens the soft prediction rather than snapping to an edge; from \(p_0\ge 50\) it snaps like annealing does. The limit object also changes: the fixed point is a local minimiser of a nonconvex piecewise-constant energy, not the unique Power Watershed, and it has no quasi-linear combinatorial evaluation; deployment is a few linear solves.

Whether that is worth a layer that costs five times the training time is a question for a task where touching objects matter more than pixel IoU.

The 20-step unrolled WS layer, i.e. the output actually trained, is 0.003 IoU below the U-Net and level on BF<sub>2</sub>; the +0.008 IoU between the two is what 20 Jacobi-PCG steps leave on the table at p = 10 with closed contours, so either K or a converged (implicit) layer at evaluation is part of the recipe. Against section 6.1’s run without the edge target, the gain is +0.005 IoU, +0.016 BF<sub>1</sub> and +0.013 BF<sub>2</sub>, paired, and F1 0.724 against 0.680: the segmentation loss alone did not find the contour costs, the edge target did (last column of the crop panels: a closed, 1-2 px contour around every nucleus and along every seam, where section 6.1’s costs were ridges inside the nuclei).<tbc>

- **It cuts more seams, but it is still mostly a denoiser, and the gain is where objects are few.** The WS layer now predicts 29 % of the seam pixels as background and cuts 19 % of the seams entirely, against 20 % / 14 % in section 6.1 and 19 % / 13 % for the gap U-Net; its own logits cut 42 % / 26 %, so the solve still closes half of what the network opens. The IoU gain is +0.012 on the 486 patches with fewer than 10 nuclei and +0.002 elsewhere, and the count error drops most on those patches (0.50 vs 0.77): the WS layer removes spurious small components and rounds off the nuclei, the mechanism of section 6.1, done better because the contours are now real. The learned edge scale fell to 0.41 (from 8, and 4.1 in section 6.1): with a clean contour probability map the network wants weak cuts at p = 10, consistent with the solve staying a smoother that respects contours rather than a cutter.<tbc>

**-** **The limit becomes usable again, at both p.** The edge target is the first thing that moves the exact Power Watershed at low p off the floor: 0.637 IoU and F1 0.682 / PQ 0.562 on the 307 limit patches against 0.508 and 0.523 / 0.435 in section 6.1 (the gap U-Net on the same patches: F1 0.645 / PQ 0.520; the converged solve: 0.698 / 0.564), with the best label-free edge alignment of any non-limit output (0.625). At p 5 \(\rightarrow\) 50 with the binary target the limit on the supervised costs scores 0.684 IoU and 0.744 BF<sub>2</sub>, its price against the converged solve shrinks to -0.016 IoU and zero BF<sub>2</sub> (from -0.046 / -0.034 in section 6), and the crops show it separating touching nuclei cleanly; but that model’s finite-p output is worse than without the target (-0.006 IoU paired, raw F1 0.45 because the closed contours leave holes and fragments at threshold), and the limit stays 0.030 IoU below the plain U-Net. So the edge target buys a deployable limit or a stronger finite-p layer depending on p, and the p 2 \(\rightarrow\) 10 solve is the better product on this data.<tbc>

**-** **The Dice-band loss removes the dotted-contour artefact and nothing else.** Both models lose 0.02 IoU and 0.03 BF<sub>2</sub> against BCE while gaining 0.03<tbc>

band accuracy: the band Dice rewards filling the 3-px band on average, which the models satisfy with a softer, wider edge (14 % soft pixels, components 31 per patch instead of 91 under the boundary-F surrogate, but still 8 too many). The gap between layer and U-Net is the same -0.005 IoU as under the boundary-F loss, reached by dragging both down. The boundary-F surrogate of section 7 with a minimum-area filter remains the better boundary loss, and adding the edge target to the Dice loss (`edge\_dice`) helps neither.<tbc>

**-** **What this does and does not establish.** One configuration, one seed, one fold pair, and a margin of 0.004-0.005 IoU with a bootstrap interval that clears zero but not by much; the instance margin (+0.06 F1, +0.05 PQ) is the robust part, and it is consistent across tissues. The result stands on three ingredients at once (gap target, low p with sharp edges, edge target), none of which helps on its own, and the comparison is against a U-Net that has no access to the edge supervision; a U-Net with a second contour head trained on the same edge target, and its contours used in a classical watershed post-processing, is the fair next baseline; section 10.1 runs it. The Pets repeat of the edge target is not possible (no instances); a boundary target from the trimap would be the analogue.

The remaining arguments for the WS layer are therefore architectural (one module, trained end to end, a limit that section 10 showed is usable again) rather than a metric margin on this dataset. The same caveats as section 10 apply, one seed and one fold pair, plus the baseline's own: the simplest marker recipe (distance-transform maxima) with one tuned spacing; a HoVer-Net-style distance or gradient head would be a stronger classical baseline still.

## P The instances are the labels: a multi-marker WS layer

So the natural use of the WS layer on nuclei is not binary nucleus / background but one label per nucleus, with the markers supplied per image. : `MultiRWLayer`, `ImplicitRWMulti`, `label\_systems`, `multi\_cross\_entropy`, `eroded\_markers`, `pw\_ limit\_multi\_numpy` / `power\_watershed\_multi` in `experiments/pw\_layer.py` (self-tests in its ` \_main\_`); `experiments/exp\_instance\_pannuke.py` (model,<tbc>

<tbc>training, evaluation), `run\_instances.sh`, `plot\_instances.py`; `instance\_metrics` of `seg\_metrics.py` accepts a label map. Raw results, per-image metrics, figures and the full tables: `results/pannuke\_instances/` (`figures/summary.md`, `run\_instances.log`; the trained model stays on jacobian).

**The WS layer.** For K markers plus the background, label k gets an attachment a\_k \(\ge\) 0 per pixel and the K + 1 systems share the matrix:

`(L(w) + diag($\\Sigma$\_j a\_j)) x\_k = a\_k, k = 0 \\dots{} K, so that $\\Sigma$\_k x\_k = 1 (L 1 = 0).`

x\_k,i is the probability that a random forest at inverse temperature p connects pixel i to label k. The systems of every image of a batch are stacked along the batch axis (M = \(\Sigma\)\_b (K\_b + 1) systems, the weights gathered per image), so the PCG of section 1 runs unchanged on (M,1,H,W) tensors, K is free per image, and the cost is affine in K with no padding. The solve is implicit; the adjoint is one solve per label with the same matrix, dl/dw\_e = -\(\Sigma\)\_k (x\_k,u - x\_k,v)(\(\lambda\)\_k,u - \(\lambda\)\_k,v) and dl/da\_k,i = \(\lambda\)\_k,i - \(\Sigma\)\_j \(\lambda\)\_j,i x\_j,i (own right-hand side, shared diagonal), which reduces to the binary formulas of section 0 for K = 1. Attachments: a\_0,i = exp(-p c0\_i) everywhere, c0 = -log(1 - s) the U-Net’s background cost; a\_k,i = exp(-p c1\_i) on the marker pixels of label k with c1 = -log s and zero elsewhere, so the markers are soft (their strength is the network’s foreground confidence) and differentiable; the edge costs are the learned cost head of sections 6.1 and 10 (scale \(\cdot\sigma(\mathrm{h})\), learnable scale, edge target).

**The limit with K labels. power\_watershed** of section 1 interpolates scalar seed values on the plateaus it has to solve, which is the exact limit for two labels only. `power\_watershed\_multi` keeps a K-vector per merged node: seeds are one-hot, a plateau that touches two distinct known vectors is solved with K right-hand sides at once (unit-weight RW), and the argmax is taken at the end, so it is the limit of the K systems above and not an interpolation of label indices. Self-tests (\(7\times\) 9 grid, random costs, K = 3; \(12\times\) 14 grid with costs quantised to 1/4 so that large ambiguous plateaus occur): the label probabilities sum to one to 1e-14, the two-label case equals the binary WS layer and the binary limit, the adjoint matches finite differences to seven digits on every input, the argmax of the finite-p solve equals the limit’s at p = 60, and on the quantised grid the K-vector limit equals the K + 1 one-hot runs of the scalar `power\_watershed` exactly.

**Training** (fold \(1\rightarrow\) fold 2 as before, 30 epochs, batch 16, one seed). The U-Net has four output channels: the foreground logit (its sigmoid s gives c0 and c1), the two-channel cost head, and a marker logit. Training markers are the ground-truth instances eroded by 2 or 3 px (radius drawn per step; the core of a nucleus the erosion would empty is kept), the marker head is trained with BCE against them, and the WS layer loss is the per-pixel cross-entropy of the K + 1 label probabilities against the instance map (the seam pixels and their 1-px flank weighted \(\times\) 6), plus 0.5 BCE on the foreground logit and section 10’s edge target (\(\times\) 1) on the cost head. p is annealed \(5\rightarrow\) 20 (section 6.1: costs learned at low p do not transfer to p = \(\infty\), so both the finite-p output and the exact limit are reported). The training solve runs to a relative residual of 1e-4 or 100 PCG<tbc>

<tbc>iterations, evaluation to 1e-5; 290 s per epoch, 2.4 h in all, 1 h for the evaluation (four solves per batch plus the CPU metrics).

**Test markers** are the 4-connected components of the thresholded marker map (0.5). Each ground-truth nucleus is counted as having exactly one, none or several predicted markers (a marker belongs to the nucleus holding the majority of its pixels), and markers in background are counted. A second variant ("fallback") adds a marker at the distance-transform maximum of every foreground component (s _\>_ 0.5, \(\ge\) 16 px) that has none. The oracle row runs the same trained costs from the ground-truth markers (eroded by 2 px): it bounds what better markers could give.

**Baselines and controls.** The plain U-Net + connected components of section 6 (binary target) and the contour-head U-Net with the tuned marker watershed of section 10.1 (the strongest pipeline so far), both re-used from their per-image files; within this model, its own foreground logits + components, the classical marker watershed (skimage) of the learned contour map inside s _\>_ 0.5 from the same predicted markers, the converged solve and the exact limit with image-gradient edge costs in place of the learned ones (the RMS colour difference across each edge, scaled per patch so that its 99th percentile equals the unary clamp 8: the marker-controlled watershed with the U-Net’s background as a soft seed), and the exact K-label limit of the learned costs on the 307 patches of section 6. Instance metrics are computed on the label maps themselves (argmax over the K + 1 labels; one predicted instance per label that wins at least one pixel), pixel metrics on the foreground (label _\>_ 0) against the binary mask, so they are comparable with section 6’s rows.
