**–** **Honest outcome: instances as labels give the WS layer a margin over the U-Net + components pipeline, not over the best classical pipeline.** The WS layer from its own markers scores F1 0.681 / PQ 0.554 / AJI 0.652: +0.024 F1, +0.023 PQ and +0.158 AJI over the plain U-Net of section 6, paired and clear of zero, with the highest edge alignment of any full-set output (0.585), and it is the first output in this report whose instances come from a single differentiable module with no post-processing at all (no threshold on the output, no component filter, no marker spacing). Against the contour-head U-Net with the tuned watershed of section 10.1 it is behind by 0.034 F1 and 0.029 PQ and level on AJI (-0.005): its segments are as tight (SQ 0.814 against 0.816) but it detects fewer nuclei correctly (DQ 0.681 against 0.715). It is also 0.013 IoU below the U-Net on the foreground, and its count error is the worst of the three (0.46: 28.6 predicted instances for 23.7 nuclei). On crowded patches (more than 60 nuclei) it is the best method, on sparse ones the worst, the reverse of the binary WS layer’s pattern in section 10.1.<tbc>

**–** **The costs are not the problem; the markers are.** With the ground-truth markers the same trained costs give F1 0.959 / PQ 0.805 / AJI 0.858 and 0.859 IoU, i.e. the WS layer assigns almost every pixel to the right nucleus once it knows where the nuclei are, and separates touching ones along the learned contours (DQ 0.959, count error 0.02; last column of `examples\_crop.png`). The oracle leaks the ground truth (the markers are its instances eroded by 2 px), so 0.96 is an upper bound and not a target, but the gap to 0.681 is entirely the marker head: 17 % of the nuclei get no marker and vanish into<tbc>

the background (this is also where the 0.013 IoU goes: patch #4 of the crops loses half its nuclei), 10 % get several and are split, and 5.9 spurious markers per patch in background become small false instances (the count error; the WS layer gives them few pixels because the background attachment is strong there, but it does not remove them). The marker head is a one-threshold blob detector trained with plain BCE on eroded masks; a HoVer-Net-style distance or centre-vector head, or a learned threshold, is the obvious next step, and the fallback markers from the foreground mask are not it (-0.024 F1: the foreground head degenerated into speckle, see below, so its components are not nuclei).<tbc>

- **The learned costs are what the WS layer contributes, and a classical watershed cannot use them as well.** The same predicted markers through the skimage marker watershed of the learned contour map inside s \> 0.5 give F1 0.597 (-0.084 paired), partly because that mask is the degenerate foreground head (723 components per patch, F1 0.024, as in section 6’s division of labour: with the background attachment taking c0 =-log(1-s) the network only needs s as a soft prior and the 0.5 auxiliary BCE did not stop it). The marker-controlled watershed with image-gradient costs, exact (0.335 F1) or at finite p (0.355), fails on H&E as `rw\_img` did in section 6: the colour gradient is not the nucleus boundary. So the classical control is far below, and the margin over it is the learned cost head plus the soft background seed, not the solver.<tbc>

- **The limit is usable again, at p = 20.** The exact K-label Power Watershed of the learned costs is within 0.008 IoU and 0.013 BF<sub>2</sub> of the converged finite- p solve on the 307 patches, with +0.007 F1 and -0.003 PQ, where section 6.1’s binary model trained at p \(\le\) 20 lost 0.2 IoU at the limit. Two reasons: the cross-entropy over markers trains the costs to put a cut between every pair of neighbouring markers, which is exactly what a maximum spanning forest needs, and the background is a soft seed (a\_0 = (1-s)^p) rather than a competing unary that has to saturate. So deploy-at-the-limit costs 0.7 s per patch on one CPU core against 224 ms per image on the GPU for the converged solve, and gives the same instances. One training caveat: the training solve hit its 100-iteration cap from epoch 9 (p ≈ 8) on, so two thirds of the training ran on a forward solve above the 1e-4 residual and an implicit gradient of an approximately solved system; the validation curves are flat from epoch 10, which is consistent with a converged model but was not checked with a higher cap. The edge scale went from 8 to 2.0 again (section 6.1).<tbc>

**- **What this says about the plan.** The multi-marker WS layer is the right object: one solve for any number of nuclei, exact limit, no post-processing hyper-parameter, and a margin of +0.02 F1 / PQ and +0.16 AJI over the pipeline a practitioner would build from the same U-Net. It does not beat a U-Net that was given a contour head and a tuned watershed, and the oracle says the reason is marker quality, which is a detection problem the WS layer does not touch. The same one-seed, one-fold-pair caveats as sections 10 and<tbc>

10.1 apply, plus the marker head’s untuned threshold and the capped training solve.

### P.1 Better markers: a tuned threshold, a distance head, and a higher solver cap

Added 18-19 October 2026 (side session). Section 11 ended with the markers as the bottleneck: the same trained costs give F1 0.959 from the ground- truth markers and 0.681 from the marker head’s. This section tries the two things it named, as options of `experiments/exp\_instance\_pannuke.py` (the defaults reproduce the section 11 run): `--mk-head dist` (a HoVer-Net-style distance head), `--tune-fold F` (the marker threshold, minimum marker area and, for the distance head, the prominence of the maxima chosen by PQ on a held-out fold, never on fold 2), `--load` (re-evaluate a saved model) and the existing `--maxit` of the training solve. `run\_instances\_11\_1.sh` launches the runs, `plot\_instances.py`\\-\\/-ref adds the section 11 run to every table, `compare\_instances.py` (numpy only) makes the cross-run tables. Results: `results/pannuke\_instances/{bce\_tuned, dist, dist\_ext, maxit300, maxit300\_tuned}/` (each with `figures/summary.md` holding all the tables of section 11 plus the tuning table, `run.log`, the per-image npz; the examples npz is kept for `dist` only), `results/pannuke\_instances/compare\_11\_1.md`.

**Choosing the post-processing on fold 3. --tune-fold 3** runs the trained model on 300 evenly spaced patches of fold 3 (neither the training nor the test fold, as the marker spacing of section 10.1), builds the markers for every setting of a grid, runs the converged WS layer from them and keeps the setting with the best PQ of the WS layer’s output; the whole table goes to the json and to the top of `summary.md`. For the BCE head of section 11 the grid is thr \(\in\{0.2\dots 0.7\}\times\) min area \(\in\{1,4,9,16\}\) px (24 settings; 50 min while sharing the GPU with a training run); for the distance head the same \(\times\) h \(\in\{0.05,0.1,0.2\}\) (72 settings, 41 min on a free GPU). The section 11 model was re-tuned this way without retraining (`bce\_tuned`: its saved `.pt` through `--eval-only --load`), to separate the effect of the threshold from the effect of the head.

**The distance head** (`dist`). Channel 3 of the U-Net predicts, through a sigmoid, the normalised distance transform of every instance: the Chebyshev distance to the instance boundary (the `label\_core\_distance` already used for the training markers, capped at 12 px) divided by the instance’s own maximum, so every nucleus is 1 at its centre and 0 at its border whatever its size, background 0; MSE loss with weight 2 in place of the BCE on eroded masks. Everything else is section 11’s recipe: the WS layer’s cross-entropy from the ground-truth markers eroded by 2-3 px, p 5 \(\rightarrow\) 20, the edge target, 30 epochs, the 100-iteration training solve. Test markers are the regional maxima of the predicted map with prominence at least h (`skimage.morphology.h\_maxima`, one seed per plateau, so saturation at 1 is harmless), grown by a watershed of the map down to the threshold thr, basins below the minimum area dropped: two touching nuclei whose maxima are separated by a valley deeper than h get two markers even when the valley is above thr. The prediction at the end of section 11.1 was right, and slightly pessimistic for the WS layer: the baseline does not merely match it, its segmentation quality is higher (SQ 0.824 against 0.811), because the foreground head of the plain U-Net is the best of the report (IoU 0.725 for its thresholded logits, +0.006 over the section 6 U-Net and +0.018 over the WS layer's output), whereas the WS layer's foreground head degenerated to speckle in both section 11 runs and its output foreground is 0.012 IoU below.<tbc>

**–** **The solver is a watershed.** With the WS layer's own markers and the WS layer's own output foreground, a marker watershed of the WS layer's contour map reproduces the converged solve on every metric to three digits (differences +0.000 with intervals of width 0.000 on 2523 patches): at p = 20 with the edge target's sharp costs, the solve assigns every pixel to the marker that the steepest path of the contour map reaches first, which is what the watershed does, as section 11.1's 0.008 F1 gap between the solve and the exact Power-Watershed limit already suggested. With the WS layer's markers inside this model's foreground the watershed is -0.010 F1 / -0.002 PQ and +0.019 IoU / +0.018 AJI against the solve: the markers decide the detections, the foreground decides the pixels, and the assignment step is immaterial. The reverse cell confirms it from the other side: this model's markers (compact cores above d = 0.5) through the WS layer's solve lose 0.058 F1 / 0.075 PQ to the same markers through the watershed, because the WS layer's degenerate foreground head gives the background label a strong attachment inside the nuclei and the compact markers do not reach far enough to win the rim; the WS layer only works with markers grown down to d = 0.2 that already cover most of each nucleus. The relief of the watershed is immaterial too (the contour map, -d and their sum agree to 0.001): the markers grown by a watershed of the distance map already decide every split between touching nuclei, and the final watershed only distributes the rim below the threshold.<tbc>

**–** **Two different marker operating points, the same detections.** Fold 3 chose a higher threshold for this model than for the WS layer (0.5 against 0.2), with a flat PQ plateau from 0.4 to 0.5, so its markers are fewer and cleaner:<tbc>

76.6 % of the nuclei with one marker, 21.8 % with none, 1.6 in background per patch, against the WS layer’s 83.9 / 14.5 % and 3.6. The detections come out the same (DQ 0.794 against 0.791) because the WS layer’s extra markers are mostly spurious ones; swapping the markers under the same watershed moves F1 by -0.014 in favour of this model’s set. Keeping the unmarked foreground components as instances recovers IoU (0.725) and AJI (0.666) but costs 0.014 F1 / 0.017 PQ, as the WS layer’s fallback markers did (-0.015 F1): the unmarked components are mostly merged clumps and fragments, not missed nuclei. On the sparse patches (fewer than 10 nuclei) the baseline is clearly ahead (F1 0.727 / count error 0.35 against 0.689 / 0.64: fewer background markers), on the crowded ones (more than 60) slightly behind (0.754 / 0.23 against 0.763 / 0.15, with 29 % of the nuclei unmarked against 22 %).<tbc>

**-** **The oracles are not comparable, and the remaining gap is still the markers.** With the ground-truth markers the watershed reaches F1 0.867 / PQ 0.708, +0.073 F1 over its predicted markers, where the WS layer’s oracle reaches 0.959: the watershed is confined to the predicted foreground, so a marker in a nucleus that s \> 0.5 missed yields nothing (count error 0.066 against the WS layer oracle’s 0.020), whereas the WS layer’s marker attachment overrides its foreground head. The 0.073 of this model’s oracle gap is the 21.8 % of the nuclei without a marker, as the 0.17 of the WS layer’s was its 14.5 %: the next step on either side is a detection objective for the distance head, not the assignment step.<tbc>

**-** **What this says about the plan.** On PanNuke, with a fair baseline on every count (the same backbone, the same three targets, post-processing tuned on a held-out fold like the WS layer’s markers), the multi-marker WS layer is not a better nucleus instance segmenter than a U-Net with a HoVer-Net-style head and a 16-ms watershed: it is 0.003 F1 behind, 0.013 PQ behind, six times slower at inference, and its foreground head degenerates. What the WS layer still offers is architectural (one differentiable module trained end to end from the instance labels, no post-processing threshold on the foreground, an exact limit within 0.01 F1), plus the one empirical fact this section adds, that at the p it trains to its solve _is_ the marker watershed of its learned contour map. The remaining caveats are those of sections 10.1 and 11.1: one seed, one fold pair, the baseline’s thresholds chosen on 300 patches of fold 3, and the foreground target of the two models identical here but different from section 10.1’s gap target (not re-run with `--gap`).

A marker head good enough to help the WS layer would have to be more precise than the watershed needs.<tbc>

**-** **What this says about the plan.** Two rounds (11.3, 11.4) of objectives on the distance head, six variants, have not moved the WS layer’s markers past the MSE-trained map of section 11.1, and the one neutral change (the gradient term) is neutral for the baseline too. The lever is not the loss on the map but what the costs are trained with: the solve has only ever been trained from ground-truth markers (section 11’s recipe), so it has never learned to confine a spurious label or to do without a missing one, and at test time it meets both. Training the solve from the predicted markers for part of the schedule, with the cross-entropy still against the true instances, is the experiment that addresses the mismatch directly; it is the next one if this thread continues. Everything here remains one seed on one fold pair.

### P.5 Training the solve from the model’s own markers

Added 23-24 October 2026 (side session; seven jobs on ruche’s A100 partition over two nights). Section 11.4 ended on the diagnosis that the lever was not the loss on the marker map but what the solve is trained with: in every run since section 11 the training markers were the ground-truth instances eroded by 2-3 px, so the costs never met a spurious marker or a missing one, while at test time 14.5 % of the nuclei have no marker and 3.6 markers per patch sit in background. This section closes that mismatch. : `--mk-sched E0 E1` in `experiments/exp\_instance\_pannuke.py`: from epoch E0 on, every training image draws, with probability (ep - E0 + 1) / (E1 - E0 + 1) rising to 1 at E1, the markers that `predicted\_markers` extracts from the current distance head (no gradient through the extraction, which runs<tbc>

<tbc>in a process pool; thresholds `--mk-train-thr 0.2`, `--mk-train-min-area 16`, `--mk-train-h 0.2`, the fold-3 choice of section 11.1) in place of the eroded ground truth (`mixed\_label\_systems`). The cross-entropy stays against the true instance map (`mapped\_cross\_entropy`): the target of a predicted label is the ground-truth nucleus holding the majority of its marker pixels (the owner rule of `marker\_quality`), so a marker in background has no pixel to win and its label is penalised wherever it wins; a nucleus with several markers keeps all of them, the probability of the target being their sum, so the loss does not force a split; the pixels of a nucleus without a marker can be right under no label and get zero weight (they stay in the denominator; `--mk-unmarked bg` makes the background label their target instead: the solve is then asked to hand an unmarked nucleus to the background rather than to a neighbour). The per-epoch log carries the schedule probability, the share of images on predicted markers, the quality of those markers on the training batches and the share of unreachable pixels (`sched\_*`, `train\_mk\_*`, `train\_unreach`, also on TensorBoard). ## Q Check of our Power Watershed limit against the authors’ reference code

Our exact limit (`power\_watershed` in `pw\_conditioning.py`, `power\_watershed\_ multi` in `pw\_layer.py`: a NumPy/SciPy re-implementation of Algorithm 1 of Couprie, Grady, Najman and Talbot, PAMI 2011) had only been validated against finite-p Random Walker solutions and against itself. It was checked against the authors' C/C++ implementation, `PW\_1.0.1` from `https://sourceforge.net/ projects/powerwatershed` (Camille Couprie, Sept 2010; PINK + CSparse), on the same problems. Harness and build notes: `experiments/pwref/` (README), records: `results/pwref/`.

**What the reference program does. powerwatsegm -a 2 -i image.pgm -s seeds.pgm** (or `-m` for a multi-label seed image, values 1..K) builds the 4- connected grid, weights w = 255-|I\_u-I\_v| (8-bit grey images; colour images use the maximum over channels), then _reconstructs_ the weights geodesically from the seeds (`grey\_weights\_PW`: the dilation of the seed-adjacent weights under the weights in the line graph, i.e. every edge's weight is lowered to the bottleneck of the best path that connects it to a seed), and runs `PowerWatershed\_q2` with the reconstructed weights for the plateau ordering and the original weights inside a plateau. A plateau is the grid-connected set of edges of equal reconstructed weight around the current maximum; inside it the edges whose original weight is higher are merged first (Kruskal, never two known nodes), and the unit-weight Random Walker is solved by a CSparse LU on the edges at the level, between merged nodes, with the seeds and the previously solved nodes as boundary. Potentials are stored in single precision. It writes `mask.pgm` (label of the largest potential; at exactly 0.5 the first label, the foreground), and `proba.pgm` = 255-255\(\cdot\)P(label 1) truncated to a byte. With `-g 1` the reconstructed weights replace the weights altogether (a different problem).

**Why the reconstruction is the algorithm, not a heuristic.** The plateau of Algorithm 1 lives in the merged graph: two equal-weight edges that touch the same merged node belong to one plateau even when they share no pixel. A breadth-first search over grid-adjacent edges of equal _raw_ weight splits such a plateau into pieces that are then solved one after the other, and the result depends on the order in which equal weights are sorted. The reconstruction lowers every interior edge of a region that is cut off from the seeds above level t to exactly t, so the reconstructed plateau at level t is grid-connected through those interior edges and is the merged-graph plateau (split at most at known nodes, which does not couple anything); the interior edges are then merged first, and the solve runs on the level-t edges between merged nodes. That is what our code does directly with a union-find over merged nodes. Both readings were verified (`check\_recon.py` reproduces the reconstructed weights of the dump exactly on 30 cases; `order\_dependence.py` runs the reference under three seeds of its unseeded `rand()`).

**Set-up.** A replacement `main` (`pwref\_wrap.cpp`) calls the reference’s own functions in the program’s order, because the third-party option parser of the release miscompiles on current clang; the released executable built on jacobian<tbc>

<tbc>(gcc 13) gives masks identical to the wrapper’s on the three 512<sup>2</sup> cases it was run on (`proba.pgm` differs by \(\pm 1\) byte on a few hundred pixels, single-precision rounding across compilers). The float potentials come from a six-line dump patch at the end of `PowerWatershed\_q2`. Both codes get the identical graph (the reference’s own edge order), the identical integer weights (our costs are 255-w = |I\_u-I\_v|, read back from the reference’s dump; the squared cost of the rest of the report is a monotone transform with the same ties, hence the same limit, and the 2<sup>-20</sup> quantisation of `pw\_limit\_numpy` plays no role with 8-bit costs) and the identical seeds. ## Q.1 A Numba back end for the limit, bit-for-bit

The profile of the NumPy limit code explains the \(10\times\) gap to the C reference: the plateau solves are negligible (a few milliseconds of the 0.6 s on camera at 512<sup>2</sup>); on 8-bit costs the time is the whole-image passes repeated at each of the ~180 cost levels (union-find compression, a sparse graph and its connected components, `np.unique`), and on continuous learned costs quantised to 2<sup>-20</sup> (246 000 plateaus on a 256<sup>2</sup> graph) it is the Python edge loop of the scalar union-find. `pw\_fast.py` compiles exactly that bookkeeping with Numba (one sorted-edge pass, path-compressed union-find over merged nodes, the components of each level in the merged graph, the merges of the unambiguous components) and hands the ambiguous plateaus back to the same NumPy/SciPy solve code as before: the same dense solve per component on levels of at most 64 edges, the same single block LU on larger levels, the same unknown ordering, the same accumulation order of the right-hand sides and the same representatives of merged components. The results are therefore identical to the bit, ties at exactly 0.5 included, which `experiments/pwref/validate\_fast.py` checks with `np.array\_equal`: 400 random coarse 24<sup>2</sup> cases (two labels and 3-5 labels, with the small-plateau path on and off), the ten 512<sup>2</sup> cases of section 1 (scalar and as a two-label K-vector solve), and the learned-cost regime on the label-augmented 256<sup>2</sup> graph at three quantisations (scalar, and 40 markers): 0 mismatches on the Mac (Python 3.14, Numba 0.68) and on jacobian (3.12), the reference-harness records of section 12 are unchanged under the new back end, and the self- tests of `pw\_layer.py` print the same limit lines under both. `power\_watershed` and `power\_watershed\_multi` pick the back end automatically (`backend=None`: Numba when importable, else NumPy; `PW\_BACKEND=numpy|numba` overrides), so `pw\_limit\_numpy` and `pw\_limit\_multi\_numpy` and every evaluation script get it without change; the first call per process compiles for about 1.5 s and the compiled code is cached on disk.

(Mac timings; jacobian is 20-30 % slower on both.) What remains is dominated by the argsort of the edges and by the solves themselves, so the limit now costs about what the authors' C code costs, and a 256<sup>2</sup> learned-cost patch goes from a second to 50 ms: cheap enough to be an inference-time operator, or to evaluate the limit on a whole fold in a minute instead of in a process pool. The NumPy version stays as the fallback and as the definition.

**The variant.** From the scheduled epochs on (`--mk-sched 10 15`, as in 11.5) the training markers are not the fold-3 markers of section 11.1 but permissive candidates: every h-maximum of the predicted distance map with prominence 0.1 above 0.1, grown down to 0.1, area 1 (`--mk-train-thr 0.1 --mk-train-h 0.1 --mk-train-min-area 1`; about 40 candidates per training image, of which 17-21 in background, against 25 markers per patch in 11.5). Every candidate k gets a strength \(\sigma\text{\_}k=\text{sigmoid}((z\text{\_}k-\theta)/\mathrm{T})\), z\_k a score of the marker logit over the candidate and \(\theta\), T two learned scalars of the model (initialised at -1 and 1), and the strength multiplies the foreground probability inside the candidate's attachment:

`a\_k,i = ($\backslashsigma$\text{\_}k\text{\_}s\text{\_}i)^p` `on the candidate’s pixels, i.e. c1\_i $\backslashto$ c1\_i $-$ log $\backslashsigma$\text{\_}k`.

The strength enters in cost units, like every other cost of the WS layer. A plain multiplier \(\sigma\text{\_}k\) on a\_k would shift the cost by only \(-log\sigma\text{\_}k/\mathrm{p}\), which at p = 20 cannot veto a marker inside a nucleus, where the background attachment (1 - s)^p is about e^-160. The cross-entropy target of a candidate follows the owner rule of 11.5 (the nucleus holding the majority of its pixels) with one change, `--ds-multi primary`: of the candidates a nucleus owns, only the one with the largest overlap is its target. A duplicate is then wrong wherever it wins and is pushed towards zero strength, exactly like a candidate in background, instead of sharing the nucleus as the 11.5 sum rule allowed. Unmarked nuclei go to the background label (`--mk-unmarked bg`), the ground-truth markers of the early epochs carry no strength (\(\sigma=1\)), and the rest of the recipe is 11.5's (`--mk-head dist --w-mk 2`, p 5 \(\rightarrow\) 20, edge target, 30 epochs, seed 0, fold 1 \(\rightarrow\) fold 2). At test time the candidates are extracted the same way, those with \(\sigma\text{\_}k\) below a cut \(\tau\) are dropped and the others enter the solve with their strengths; fold 3

**Gradient check. --ds-selftest** runs the training loss (mixed systems with the primary rule and the background target, seam-like weights, p = 8) in float64 on two \(10\times 12\) images with two nuclei each and six candidates (primaries, a duplicate, two in background, one unmarked nucleus), and compares the implicit adjoint with central finite differences (\(\varepsilon\) = 1e-6, solve to a relative residual of 1e-12): d/d\(\theta\), d/d log T, d/d(marker logit) at every pixel, and two random directions in each of the edge costs, c0, c1 and the marker logit. Worst relative error 6.0e-7 for the mean score, 3.0e-8 for the maximum (`ds\_selftest.txt`). The signs are the intended ones: the background candidates get dL/dz _\>_0 (weaken), the primary of the image whose nucleus is contested gets dL/dz _\<_0. A candidate that wins or loses its pixels outright gets a gradient of 1e-11 or less, because the Random Walker probabilities are saturated in its attachment. Checked on the trained 11.5 model before launching (32 training patches, p = 20, \(\theta\) = -1, T = 1): every one of the 227 background candidates and the 39 duplicates is pushed weaker, 83 % of the 582 primaries stronger; the 64 % of background candidates with a negligible gradient are those that win no pixel, so they cost nothing.

**First run: the peak score fragments the marker map** (`dist\_ds\_max`, z\_k = maximum of the logit over the candidate, the candidate of the brief). From the first scheduled epoch the candidates multiplied: background candidates per training image \(21\rightarrow 63\rightarrow 123\) over epochs 10-12, duplicates per epoch \(1.5\text{k}\rightarrow 13\text{k}\rightarrow 47\text{k}\), and the epoch time \(221\rightarrow 371\rightarrow 723\) s. The job was stopped at epoch 12; at that rate it would not have finished training within the 12-hour job. The cause is the needle failure of section 11.3’s raw-maximum peak loss, mirrored: the whole gradient of a candidate goes to its arg-max pixel, and pushing that one pixel down splits the peak into neighbouring maxima, each a new candidate. The run reported below uses the mean of the logit over the candidate (`--ds-peak mean`, the default): the gradient shifts the whole candidate uniformly, which cannot create a maximum inside it, and the push per pixel is |R\_k| times smaller. With it the candidate counts stayed flat (17-21 background candidates per image from epoch 10 to 29), at 320-340 s per epoch against 189 s before the schedule (17 s of candidate extraction, more systems per batch).

- **The selection was not learned; the detector was damaged.** Three facts. (1) The learned strengths barely discriminate: on fold 2 every candidate has \(\sigma\ge 0.5\) (background 0.64, primary 0.69, duplicate 0.68 on average), so the cut \(\tau\le 0.5\) removes nothing (`layer\_all` equals `layer` to every digit and the fold-3 table is flat in \(\tau\) up to 0.5, then collapses at 0.7). The mean background strength is weaker than the mean primary's by only a factor (0.64 / 0.69)^20≈0.2 in the attachment. (2) The ranking the strengths could use is no better than that of a head trained on its own target: AUC 0.876 against 0.867 for `dist\_sched10\_bg` and 0.874 for `unet\_dist` (primary vs background), 0.666 against 0.707 and 0.715 (primary vs duplicate). (3) The gradient that reaches the marker logits through the solve made the head a worse detector: three times as many background candidates (19.9 against 6.6 per patch at thr 0.1), a fifth fewer primaries (17.7 against 21.5), MSE to its distance target 0.022 against 0.008. What pushes the true nuclei's maps down was not isolated. A plausible route, unverified: a candidate grown down to 0.1 over two touching nuclei is the primary of one and wrong over the other, so the loss pushes the whole merged candidate down. Three of these facts point the same way. The partition cross-entropy is a weak and partly misdirected detection signal. It can tell the solve to give a spurious marker fewer pixels, which the 11.5 recipe already does through the unary costs (the variant's solve absorbs 12.6 background candidates per patch at a count error of 0.22). It cannot tell the marker head where a nucleus is that no candidate covers, since an unmarked nucleus sends no gradient to the head.<tbc>

- **The strengths live in the finite-p softness, which the limit removes.** The exact Power Watershed of the same costs and strengths gives F1 0.115 on the 307 limit patches (11.5: 0.700). At p \(\rightarrow\infty\) the shift -log \(\sigma\text{\_}\mathrm{k}\approx 0.4\) cost units turns into a hard threshold: a marker loses its whole nucleus to the background seed as soon as a path through the nucleus reaches a pixel whose background cost is below c1 + 0.4 without crossing a higher edge cost, where at p = 20 the shift only rescales the attachment by \(\sigma^\text{^}\mathrm{p}\). Deploying this variant at the limit is not possible. The oracle with ground-truth markers rises to 0.931 (11.5: 0.872), for a related reason: ground-truth markers carry \(\sigma=1\), i.e. attachments e^7 times stronger than any marker the trained solve has seen, so they override the background as the section 11 oracle did. It is not comparable with the other oracles.<tbc>

**- **What this says about the plan.** Within this design (attachment-level strengths fed by the marker head's score, trained only by the partition cross- entropy), putting marker selection in the gradient path does not let end-to-end training through the WS layer beat the U-Net + watershed pipeline; it hurts at full data and is neutral at 10 %. The bottleneck stays detection (which nuclei get a marker at all), and the WS layer's gradient is the wrong signal for it. For the paper, the statement it supports: _making marker selection_

<tbc>_differentiable (candidate strengths trained through the solve) did not help; the gradient reaching the marker head degraded detection without improving the ranking of candidates._ Untried within the deadline, in decreasing order of promise: stopping the gradient into the marker head and training only \(\theta\), T (this reduces to a learned threshold on z, i.e. the fold-3 tuning, so a small gain at best); a separate strength channel trained only by the solve, so the distance head keeps its target; and a per-image normalisation of the strengths. One seed, one fold pair, one parametrisation (mean score, \(\theta_0=-1\), primary rule).

<tbc>The U-Net forward takes 1.7 ms for one image and 14.5 ms for a batch of 16 (0.9 ms per image). The exact K-label limit on one CPU core (median over 4 patches \(\times\) 3 runs, each back end in its own process pinned to one core, the same costs and markers as the GPU runs):

- **The cost is affine in K, once the GPU is busy.** At a fixed number of PCG steps (the training setting, which hits its 100-step cap at every K here) the forward time of a batch of 16 is 41 + 20.3 K ms for K = 8-128, within 1 % of the fit at every point; a PCG step costs 12.8-14 \(\mu\)s per 256<sup>2</sup> system as soon as a batch carries more than about 150 systems, and the backward pass (one adjoint solve with the same matrix) costs the same as the forward. Below that the GPU is launch-bound: 0.34 ms per step whatever the number of systems, so one image costs the same for K = 1 and K = 16. Memory is exactly linear in the number of systems: 4.8 MB per marker per image for forward + backward, the same at batch 1 and 16 and for both settings (it is the stacked (M,1,H,W) tensors of PCG and the saved solution), i.e. 9.8 GB for a batch of 16 images with 128 markers each. "Affine in K" is therefore true of the work and of the memory, with the caveat that small problems do not fill the GPU (figure `multi\_k.png` (a, b)).<tbc>

**-** **Converged, the cost grows more slowly than K,** because more markers make the systems better conditioned: the forward needs 464 PCG steps per batch at K = 1 and 254 at K = 128 (to 1e-5). The adjoint needs about twice the forward’s steps (995 \(\rightarrow\) 519), presumably because the cross-entropy’s gradient -1/x is a rougher right-hand side than the attachments; at K = 1-2 it reaches the 1000-step cap. So the converged forward + backward of a batch of 16 goes from 0.57 s (K = 1) to 6.2 s (K = 32) and 20 s (K = 128).<tbc>

**-** **The limit is flat in K.** One CPU core computes the exact K-label Power Watershed of a 256<sup>2</sup> patch in 29 ms at K = 1 and 51 ms at K = 128 with the Numba back end (1.8 \(\times\) for 128 \(\times\) the labels; presumably the K-vector plateau solves and the K extra label nodes, not profiled), and in 0.85-0.88 s with the NumPy one (+4 %). At the K of real patches (≈ 30) the limit on one core (33 ms) is 2.4 times faster than the converged GPU solve of one image (78 ms) and 3.7 times faster than its per-image cost in a batch of 16 (123 ms); it is 20-35 times the U-Net’s forward (1.7 ms alone, 0.9 ms per image in a batch). The claim "one spanning forest whatever K" holds as stated, and with the Numba back end the limit is the cheapest way to run the trained layer.

- **Why, plausibly:** at p \(\ge\) 20 the unrolled gradient points 40-50\(^\circ\) away from the true one (cosine 0.67-0.75), so for the last two thirds of the schedule the cost head was trained against a derivative that is not that of the WS layer it is evaluated with. The run cannot separate this from the other difference between the modes, that the implicit layer is the converged solve also in the forward pass (the unrolled models are evaluated close to their converged solve too: layer = converged within 0.002 IoU).<tbc>

- **The exact limit does not benefit, it suffers.** On the 307 limit patches the limit of the implicit-trained costs loses 0.107-0.108 IoU against their converged solve (0.60 against 0.71) and has the worst count error of the four runs (0.39-0.42), where the unrolled runs’ limits lose 0.039 and 0.083 IoU and vary a lot between seeds (0.668 / 0.620). Learning the costs at the true finite-p solution makes the model rely on finite-p softness that the limit removes (section 6.1 saw the same with costs learned at low p). Deploy-at-the-limit therefore needs its own training consideration (higher final p, or a sharper cost parametrisation) whichever differentiation mode is used.<tbc>

- **What this says for the paper.** The three efficiency claims hold, measured: memory independent of depth for the implicit mode (92 MB for a batch of 16 at any tolerance, against 24 MB per unrolled step), cost affine in K at a fixed number of PCG steps (20.3 ms per marker per batch of 16, 4.8 MB per marker per image) with fewer steps needed as K grows, and an exact limit flat in K (29-51 ms on one core with Numba for K = 1-128). The implicit mode also wins on gradient accuracy (1e-3 against 0.9 relative error at the training p, K = 20) and on trained accuracy (+0.02 BF<sub>2</sub>, +0.03-0.05 F1 and PQ on two seeds), at twice the training time. Caveats to state: the affine law needs a batch large enough to fill the GPU (about 150 systems on an A100; below that the cost per step is flat), the converged adjoint of the multi-marker WS layer takes about twice the forward’s steps, and the limit of implicit-trained binary costs is worse than that of unrolled-trained ones.

## U Selection without touching the marker head: a strength channel, a detached scorer, and the control (follow-up of section 14)

Section 14 left two explanations for its loss, and the paper is due the next day. One: the solve’s gradient reached the distance head through the candidates’ scores and degraded it as a detector. Two: the partition cross-entropy does not supply a selection signal at all. The first can be removed without giving up the strengths, and one of us asked for a differentiable way to find markers that does. Two scorers keep the distance head out of the solve’s gradient, and a control separates the<tbc>

<tbc>scorers from the other changes of section 14 (the permissive candidates and the primary rule for duplicates). : `--ds-score head|mlp|none` in `experiments/ exp\_instance\_pannuke.py` (`scorer\_strengths`, `candidate\_features`, `unit\_ strengths`, `scorer\_selftest`), the cases `dist\_dsh`, `dist\_dsm`, `dist\_dsn` of `ruche\_run.sh`, and `candidate\_auc.py`, which now also ranks by the strength channel and the scorer. Results: `results/pannuke\_instances/{dist\_dsh, dist\_dsm, dist\_dsn}/`, `compare\_16.md`.

**The three runs.** All three keep section 14’s recipe otherwise: candidates at thr 0.1 / h 0.1 / area 1 from epoch 10 (all images from 15), primary-overlap target for duplicates, unmarked nuclei to the background label, the strength entering as a\_k = (\(\sigma\)\_k s)^p, p 5 \(\rightarrow\) 20, 30 epochs, seed 0, fold 1 \(\rightarrow\) fold 2. Fold 3 chooses thr \(\in\{0.05,0.1,0.2\}\times\) h \(\in\{0.1,0.2\}\) (area 1) and \(\tau\in\{0,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9\}\).

- `dist\_dsh` (`--ds-score head`): a fifth U-Net output channel g; \(\sigma\)\_k = sigmoid((mean of g over the candidate \(-\theta\)) / T). The distance channel gets no gradient from the solve; the shared trunk does, through g.<tbc>

- `dist\_dsm` (`--ds-score mlp`, the design proposed by the main session): a two-layer MLP (9 \(\rightarrow\) 32 \(\rightarrow\) 1, its own parameters only, output bias initialised at +4 so that \(\sigma\approx 0.98\) at the start) on nine features computed from the detached distance map d, foreground s and contour map c. The features: peak of d, relative prominence (peak - saddle) / peak, log area, mean s, mean c, whether the candidate has an adjacent candidate, and for the least-separated adjacent candidate the mean and maximum of c along the shared boundary and the relative depth of the d valley between the two peaks. log \(\sigma\)\_k = -softplus(-logit). No gradient from the strengths reaches the U-Net at all; the scorer learns only from the partition cross-entropy through the solve.<tbc>

**-** `dist\_dsn` (`--ds-score none`): every strength 1. Same candidates, same targets, no selection: the control.

**Checks.** The scorer’s gradient against central finite differences (`--ds-selftest --ds-score mlp`, the case of section 14 with the candidates’ real features from random maps, a test scorer with 8 hidden units and output bias 0.5): worst relative error 1.1e-8 over four random directions in its 89 parameters and on the output bias (`dist\_dsm/ds\_selftest\_mlp.txt`). The wiring check, on eight fold-1 patches, backpropagates the solve’s loss alone. With `head`, the distance channel’s output weights get a gradient of exactly 0 and the strength channel’s 0.19; with section 14’s scoring the distance channel gets 0.22. The sanity check proposed for the run itself, that the distance head stays at the 11.5 level, holds: its final MSE is 0.0085 (`head`), 0.0083 (`mlp`), 0.0082 (control) against 0.0082 for `dist\_sched10\_bg` and 0.0219 for section 14’s `dist\_ds`.

- **Honest outcome: neither scorer helps, and the inclusion bar for the paper is not met.** With the distance head protected, the loss of section 14 (-0.063 F1) shrinks to -0.006 (MLP scorer) and -0.013 (strength channel) against the 11.5 recipe, every interval still clear of zero and on the wrong side. Against the fair baseline the MLP scorer is -0.004 F1 / -0.011 PQ and +0.007 AJI. The bar set for the paper, a paired gain over `dist\_sched10\_bg` above the seed spread of 0.008 F1, is missed by about 0.014 F1. So section 14’s damage was the gradient into the detector, as diagnosed, but removing it leaves no gain to collect. The control apportions what is left. Training on the permissive candidates with the primary rule but no strengths (`dist\_dsn`) is itself -0.005 F1 / -0.004 PQ against 11.5 on fold 2, though level on fold 3 (PQ 0.656 against 0.655). The detached scorer adds nothing to it (-0.001 F1, interval across zero; +0.003 AJI). The strength channel subtracts 0.008 F1, presumably through the gradient it sends into the shared trunk. The learned selection is worth zero; the small loss is the candidate rule.<tbc>

**-** **What the scorers learn is not selection.** Both strengths rank background candidates _above_ true nuclei (AUC 0.11-0.13). This is not a bug: a background candidate in low-foreground territory wins no pixel at any \(\sigma\le 1\), gets no gradient, and keeps whatever strength the shared weights give it. The gradient goes to candidates that do win pixels, mostly primaries whose region (grown down to the candidate threshold) spills over the nucleus rim, and it weakens<tbc>

<tbc>them. The strengths therefore act as a per-nucleus correction of the unary at the rim, which the foreground head already provides per pixel. The one ranking that matters for the output, primaries above duplicates (the duplicates do win pixels), is not learned either (AUC 0.34-0.41). The partition cross-entropy rewards a marker for the pixels it takes, not for being a nucleus. Saturation (gradient 1e-11 for a candidate that wins or loses its pixels outright, section 14) leaves exactly the decisive cases unsupervised.<tbc>

**-** **The limit collapses again.** The exact Power Watershed with the learned strengths gives F1 0.10-0.16 on the 307 limit patches: any \(\sigma\text{\_}k<1\) is a hard veto at p \(\rightarrow\infty\) (section 14), and here every candidate sits at \(\sigma\approx 0.75\)-0.83. Strengths of this kind are incompatible with deploying the limit (the control, at \(\sigma=1\), keeps 0.611 / 0.502). The scorers’ oracles, 0.917-0.927 against 0.856 for the control, are inflated the same way as section 14’s: ground-truth markers enter at \(\sigma=1\), stronger than any marker the trained solve has seen.<tbc>

**-** **For the paper.** The section 14 sentence stands and can be sharpened: _making marker selection differentiable did not help. Strengths computed from the marker head degraded its detections (-0.063 F1), and scorers isolated from it, a strength channel or a detached per-candidate network, were still 0.006-0.013 F1 behind training the solve on the extracted markers alone, because the partition loss rewards a marker for the pixels it takes, not for being a nucleus._ The marker extraction stays a discrete step inside the training loop (paper commit 8988128). One seed, one fold pair, one design each.

4.4, which answers the request for "a figure of accuracy vs p, from the training p to the limit, for the learned costs"). : `experiments/p\_sweep.py` (the sweep), `experiments/rw\_exact.py` (an exact solve of the WS layer’s system at any p, below), `experiments/plot\_p\_sweep.py`, `experiments/run\_p\_sweep.sh` (jacobian), `experiments/ruche\_p\_sweep.sh` (CPU pass on a ruche `cpu\_med` node), `experiments/cond\_exact.py` (the section 1 check at the end). Results: `results/pannuke\_p\_sweep/` (`p\_sweep.png` / `.pdf`, `p\_sweep\_tables.md` with every table below in full, per model `p\_sweep.json`, `p\_sweep\_perimage.npz`, `pcg\_stats.npz`, `labels\_examples.npz` with the label maps at every p for 16 patches; logs on jacobian / ruche only); `results/conditioning/cond\_exact\_ 512.json`.

**Protocol.** For each trained model, the U-Net costs of every fold-2 patch are computed once (fp32 on the GPU, as in every evaluation of the report). For the multi-marker model the test markers are fixed too: the fold-3 choice of section 11.5, no fallback, i.e. its `layer` output. Only p changes, through w = exp(-p c), so the sweep isolates the temperature. At each p the WS layer’s linear system is solved exactly, and the result is compared with the exact K-label (or binary) PW limit of the same costs and markers (`pw\_limit\_multi\_numpy` / `pw\_limit\_numpy`, Numba). Models: `dist\_sched10\_bg` (section 11.5, p annealed \(5\rightarrow 20\), implicit<tbc>

<tbc>solve; the paper’s headline), `rw\_learned` (section 6, binary, p 5 \(\rightarrow\) 50, 20 unrolled PCG steps) and `edge\_bce` (section 10, `rw\_learned` with the edge target). All 2523 patches at every p, for p \(\in\{5,10,20,35,50,100,200,500\}\) (binary: no 35). Metrics as in section 12.2. The disagreement is the fraction of all pixels whose label differs from the limit’s, and in brackets the same count divided by the pixels that are foreground in either output.

**The WS layer’s PCG does not reach large p, and neither does sparse LU, so the finite-p curve needs its own solver.** On 256 evenly spaced patches the WS layer’s own converged solve (Jacobi-PCG, tol 1e-5, at most 1000 iterations, as in every evaluation) was run in fp32 and fp64 and compared with the exact solve. For the instance model it is exact up to the training p: 0 pixels differ at p \(\le\) 10, 0.015 % at p = 20, where it takes 189 iterations on average (435 at most), and every fp64 system converges. In fp32 at p = 20 the true residual stalls around 1e-3 (rounding: the recursive residual meets the tolerance, the true one cannot), with no effect on the labels. From p = 35 it degrades (0.5 % of the pixels differ), and from p = 100 it fails in both precisions: it stops at the iteration cap, true residuals reach 1e5-1e8, 5-12 % of the pixels are wrong, and F1 is 0.27-0.53 instead of 0.72 at p = 200-500. fp32 additionally floors 6-20 % of the edge weights at 1e-30. The binary models fare better because their edge costs are \(\le\) 1: `rw\_learned`’s PCG is exact to 0.001 % of the pixels up to p = 200 and wrong on 0.44 % at p = 500. For `edge\_bce`, 0.8-3.3 % of the pixels are wrong at p = 100-500, and since the thresholded output is then speckled, its F1 collapses (0.24 at p = 100 against 0.53). A diagonally rescaled sparse LU (scipy, fp64) agrees with the exact solve up to p = 100 (4 pixels over 32 patches differ there), but beyond that it loses the pivots to cancellation (d\_a-w\_ai<sup>2</sup>/d\_i of two nearly equal numbers): at p = 500 it returns negative probabilities and labels that depend on the ordering. `rw\_exact.ExactRW` solves the same system by Gaussian elimination in the Grassmann-Taksar-Heyman form, on a nested-dissection order of the grid: eliminating node i adds w\_ai w\_ib / d\_i to the remaining weights and w\_ai e\_i / d\_i to the attachment (excess) of a, and the pivot is never updated by subtraction but recomputed as the sum of the current weights and excess. Every operation is between positive numbers, so the result is accurate to rounding whatever the conditioning. The weights are held as logarithms (logadexp), and so are the label vectors of the substitution (a log scale per node), so nothing underflows. The symbolic factorisation depends on the grid only (2.6 M entries at 256<sup>2</sup>, 12.5 M at 512<sup>2</sup>), and a solve takes 1.3-1.9 s on one core at any p. Checks: \(\Sigma\)\_k x\_k = 1 to 1e-13 at every p. Its labels are identical to the WS layer’s PCG wherever the PCG converges (0 pixels at p \(\le\) 10 on the 256 patches, 0.015 % at p = 20), and to the sparse LU on 32 patches per model at every p \(\le\) 100 (4 pixels over 32 patches differ at p = 100 for the instance model, where the LU is at the edge of its accuracy). The disagreement with `pw\_limit\_multi\_numpy` falls to 0 pixels at p = 3000 on the three patches tried, which also confirms the limit code independently of section 12.

## W A detection head for the markers: CenterNet-style centres and radii

Sections 11.3, 11.4, 14 and 16 all tried to improve the markers through the distance map (a per-nucleus peak loss, hard negatives, the gradient term, strengths trained by the partition loss) and none helped; with ground-truth markers both the WS layer and the fair baseline reach F1 0.87 against 0.795 / 0.794 with their own, so marker detection is the whole remaining gap, and it is shared. one of us proposed a detection formulation instead: predict a centre and a radius per nucleus as a detector does (CenterNet / Mask R-CNN), aggregate the overlapping proposals, and use the disc as the marker. This section implements it for both models and measures it at full data and at 10 % of fold 1. : `--mk-head center` in `experiments/exp\_instance\_pannuke. py` (`center\_target`, `center\_focal\_loss`, `markers\_from\_center` with `center\_ peaks` / `disc\_iou`, `center\_strengths`; `marker\_loss` now returns the loss and its parts; the training-time extraction worker takes a dict; new outputs `layer\_soft` / `layer\_hard`) and `exp\_unet\_dist.py` (`DistSegmenter(center=True)`, `own\_ markers`), the checks `center\_check.py`, the cases `ctr\_bg`, `ctr\_bg\_soft`, `unet\_ ctr`, `ctr\_bg\_p10`, `ctr\_bg\_soft\_p10`, `unet\_ctr\_p10` of `ruche\_run.sh` and `run\_ center.sh` (jacobian / dvaughan), and the tables `compare\_center.py`. Results: `results/pannuke\_instances/{ctr\_bg, ctr\_bg\_soft, unet\_ctr}/`, `results/pannuke\_data\_efficiency/- ctr\_bg\_soft\_p10, unet\_ctr\_p10}/`, `compare\_18.md` and `compare\_18\_p10.md`, `center\_check.txt`; the `.pt` files stay on ruche / dvaughan.

**The head.** Two output channels replace the distance channel: the centre heatmap logit (channel 3, so that it is the marker map everywhere else in the code) and the radius (channel 4, softplus, in pixels). Targets from the instance masks, after the d4 augmentation: the centre pixel of every nucleus is its pixel nearest its centroid; the heatmap is the maximum over the nuclei of a Gaussian at the centre pixel with \(\sigma=\) clip(0.5 r\_eq, 1, 6) px, r\_eq = sqrt(area / \(\pi\)) the equivalent radius (mean 9.8 px on fold 1, 5 / 50 / 95 % 3.6 / 8.6 / 20.8), exactly 1 at the centres; the radius target is r\_eq at the centre pixels. Losses: the CornerNet / CenterNet focal loss on the heatmap (positives = the centre pixels, every other pixel a negative weighted (1 - target)^4, the (1 - p)^2 / p^2 modulation, normalised by the number of centres: explicit negatives everywhere, which is what the distance-map losses of 11.3-11.4 could not give without conflicting with the rim) and \(0.1\times\) the L1 of the radius at the centres; the marker-head weight is 1 (the focal loss is of order 1 after the first epoch, where the distance MSE was \(0.008\times 2\)). Foreground head, contour head and edge target unchanged.

**The marker rule.** Peaks = the pixels at the maximum of their \(3\times 3\) window and above a threshold, one per plateau; a greedy non-maximum suppression over the predicted discs (in decreasing peak order, a peak whose disc has IoU above `nms` with a kept disc is merged into it); marker k = the disc of radius `rfac` \(\times\) predicted radius (at least 1 px) around the peak, a pixel inside two discs going to the stronger, every marker keeping its peak pixel; optionally clipped to the foreground s _\>_0.5 (not used: the WS layer’s attachment c1 = -log s already makes a background disc pixel inert, and the watershed baseline’s markers lie<tbc>

<tbc>inside the foreground mask anyway). Fold 3 chooses threshold \(\in\{0.2,0.3,0.4,0.5\}\times\text{nms}\in\{0.3,0.5,0.7\}\times\text{rfac}\in\{0.3,0.5,0.7\}\) by PQ on the usual 300 patches, for the WS layer (through its converged solve) and for the baseline (\(\times\) the three reliefs), never on fold 2. The training-time markers of the 11.5 schedule use threshold 0.3, nms 0.5, rfac 0.5. At most 256 peaks per patch enter the suppression (an untrained heatmap has thousands).

**The soft variant** (`--ctr-soft`, run `ctr\_bg\_soft`). Every marker enters the attachment with its peak value as a strength, a\_k = (\(\sigma\text{\_}\text{k}\) s)^p, i.e. c1 - log \(\sigma\text{\_}\text{k}\) on its pixels as in section 14, but \(\sigma\text{\_}\text{k}\) is a constant: the detection loss alone trains it, nothing flows from the solve into the selection (the failure mode of 14). The strengths are on at training time (on the predicted markers of the schedule) and at test time. In addition every centre run evaluates the other variant on the same markers and costs (`layer\_soft` for a hard-trained model, `layer\_hard` for a soft-trained one), so the test-time effect of the strengths is separated from the training effect.

**Checks before the runs** (`center\_check.py`, 16 evenly spaced patches of fold 1; `center\_check.txt`). The targets: one centre pixel per instance (565 for 565), all inside their instance, 565 heatmap peaks for 565 instances. The rule on the target heatmap and radius (an ideal prediction): every nucleus gets exactly one marker and no marker lands in background at rfac 0.3 / 0.5 / 0.7 (marker pixels inside their own nucleus 100 / 99.9 / 98.3 %), and the same on a blurred target with the radius spread over the Gaussian's support, with or without the suppression. A baseline trained for six epochs on the full fold gave, at threshold 0.3, 29 markers per patch for 35 nuclei (74 % of the nuclei with exactly one, 25 % none, 2.3 in background; threshold 0.2: 39 markers, 85 / 11 %, 5.8 in background), the radius within 1.06 px of the target on average, and the suppression changing the count by at most 0.4 markers per patch: the head produces about one peak per nucleus, not the hundreds of section 11.3, and the threshold trades recall against background markers smoothly.

**What was run** (seed 0, fold 1 \(\rightarrow\) fold 2, tuning on fold 3, all 2523 test patches). The WS layer with the section 11.5 recipe and the centre head in place of the distance head (`ctr\_bg`: `--mk-head center --w-mk 1 --mk-sched 10 15 --mk-unmarked bg`, p 5 \(\rightarrow\) 20, edge target; the predicted markers of the schedule at threshold 0.3 / nms 0.5 / rfac 0.5), its soft-strength variant (`ctr\_bg\_soft`), the fair baseline with the same head (`unet\_ctr`: the section 11.2 U-Net and watershed, the distance channel replaced by the heatmap and radius), and the three at 10 % of fold 1 (`ctr\_bg\_p10`, `ctr\_bg\_soft\_p10`, `unet\_ctr\_p10`: 266 images, 300 epochs, `--mk-sched 100 150`, as section 13). The references are `dist\_sched10\_bg` and `unet\_dist` (sections 11.5 / 11.2) and `dist\_bg\_p10` / `unet\_dist\_p10` (section 13). The WS layer runs took 3.7 h on an A100 (326 s per epoch, 36 settings \(\times\) 300 patches of fold-3 tuning through the solve in 31 min, the evaluation with its four converged solves per batch in 85 min); the baselines 11 s per epoch; the 10 % layer runs 1.3 h for the 300 epochs. Two layer jobs died at start on ruche's node gpu16 with "CUDA-capable device busy or unavailable" and were resubmitted elsewhere; the 10 % runs ran on dvaughan.

background label, whose attachment is untouched, takes most of the nucleus: `ctr\_bg\_soft` keeps 10.5 instances per patch whatever the threshold (fold 3 gives PQ 0.476-0.478 from thr 0.2 to 0.5: the strengths _are_ the threshold), F1 0.566, and the training cross-entropy climbs from 0.10 at epoch 9 to 0.57 at epoch 29 as p anneals, because no cost the network controls can compensate a factor it cannot exceed (s \(\le\) 1). Solving the same model without the strengths recovers 0.660, and the oracle at \(\sigma\) = 1 inflates to 0.925 as in sections 14 and 16 (ground-truth markers enter stronger than any the solve was trained on). At 10 % the same recipe costs less (0.736 against 0.751, the hard solve of the soft-trained model 0.751: the training is not damaged, only the test-time veto remains), because fold 3 picks threshold 0.5 and the surviving markers have \(\sigma\ge 0.5\). The fairer version of the idea, the confidence entering as \(\sigma\text{\_}\text{k}\) itself rather than \(\sigma\text{\_}\text{k}^\text{^}\text{p}\) (`--ctr-soft-pow 1`, a cost shift of \(-(log\sigma\text{\_}\text{k})/\text{p}\), evaluated on the hard-trained `ctr\_bg` without retraining), removes the collapse but still loses 0.024 F1 / 0.018 PQ to the hard solve on the same markers and costs (added after the commit of the section, the evaluation having finished on its own): a confidence below 1 can only weaken a marker, so it cannot add recall, and the markers it weakens most are the faint true nuclei the head was least sure of. So where the watershed needs a hard threshold the WS layer needs one too: a confidence below 1 can only weaken a marker, and what the markers lack is recall, not precision. The exact limit tells the same story as section 14: any \(\sigma\text{\_}\text{k}\) \< 1 is a hard veto at p \(\rightarrow\infty\) (0.369 F1 for the soft model against 0.699 for the hard one).<tbc>

**-** **Verdict.** A CenterNet-style head is a sound marker detector for this pipeline (one peak per nucleus, a radius within 0.7 px of the target, no needle failure, the threshold trading recall against background markers smoothly), and it is the first marker change since section 11.5 that does not cost the WS layer anything; but it does not improve it. The WS layer's result is pinned at F1 0.795 by a third marker head, which says that the ceiling is not the head's form but the detectability of the 12-20 % of nuclei that none of the heads, nor the baseline, finds at a threshold that keeps the background clean: the oracle gap of 0.07 F1 is shared by every variant. For the watershed baseline the distance head stays the right choice, because it doubles as the relief. The 10 % lead of the structured layer survives the change of head (+0.006 against the distance baseline, +0.031 against the matched one) but is largest with the distance head. One seed, one fold pair, one set of hyper-parameters (\(\sigma\) = 0.5 r\_eq, focal weight 1, radius weight 0.1) for the head; a lower marker-head weight or a second seed were not run.

## X Implementation and compute

Everything runs in PyTorch on one NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada (48 GB). The WS layer uses dense shifted-grid operators (\(B\times 1\times H\times W\) tensors), Jacobi- preconditioned conjugate gradients, single precision for the unrolled mode and double precision for the reference solves. The exact limit is NumPy on the CPU,<tbc>

<tbc>about 2 s per 256<sup>2</sup> patch with continuous costs. Training the binary WS layer on a PanNuke fold costs 11 s per epoch for the unrolled mode and 50 s for the reweighted mode; the multi-marker WS layer about 230 s per epoch with 20–60 PCG iterations per batch.
